q: What is MSInfo32 (System Information) best used for?
options: Defragmenting and optimizing hard drives and solid-state drives on a schedule
Resetting a forgotten password for a local administrator or standard account
Viewing a complete inventory of hardware, components, and the software environment
Updating the motherboard BIOS or UEFI firmware to the manufacturer's latest build
explain: System Information centralizes hardware resources, components, drivers, and environment details that are valuable for diagnosis and support tickets.

q: How does Performance Monitor differ from Task Manager?
options: It can end unresponsive tasks and processes more quickly than Task Manager can
It can log specific counters over time in data collector sets for later analysis
It displays a much shorter and simpler list of processes than Task Manager does
It replaces Event Viewer as the primary tool for reading Windows event logs
explain: Performance Monitor records chosen counters such as CPU, disk, and memory over hours or days, while Task Manager mainly shows real-time values.

q: How does Resource Monitor help diagnose a hung application?
options: It lets you analyze the wait chain to see what the process is blocked on
It forces a Windows update to fix the hang
It clears the DNS cache for the application
It reinstalls the application automatically
explain: Resource Monitor's Analyze Wait Chain shows whether a process is waiting on another process or a resource, which identifies the real cause of the hang.

q: Which Settings area replaced most Control Panel applets for everyday configuration in Windows 11?
options: The Microsoft Store
Windows Admin Center only
Server Manager
The Settings app (with Control Panel still present for legacy items)
explain: Windows 10/11 moved most configuration into Settings; some advanced applets remain in Control Panel.

q: Why do User Account Control prompts appear on the dimmed secure desktop?
options: To make elevation prompts load more quickly
To hide the prompt from administrator accounts
To prevent malware from silently approving its own elevation prompt
To allow standard users to elevate without credentials
explain: The secure desktop isolates the consent prompt from normal processes, so only a real user at the keyboard can approve or deny the elevation.

q: What does Credential Manager store for a user?
options: The computer's BIOS administrator password
Saved web credentials, Windows credentials, and certificates
Wi-Fi profiles belonging to every user only
The default printer settings for the device
explain: Credential Manager vaults saved sign-in secrets, including web and Windows credentials and certificate-based credentials, for the signed-in user.

q: Why is Windows Sandbox useful for testing an untrusted application?
options: It runs the app in a disposable, isolated Windows environment that resets when closed
It permanently installs a second, fully licensed copy of Windows on the same PC
It makes the host operating system and all of its applications run noticeably faster
It replaces the need for antivirus and anti-malware software on the host machine
explain: Sandbox starts a clean, temporary Windows instance; everything installed or changed inside it is discarded when the window is closed.

q: How does a user change which program opens PDF files by default?
options: Through the Action menu in Disk Management
By creating a scheduled task in Task Scheduler
Only by editing associations in Registry Editor
In Settings under Apps and Default apps, by file type
explain: Default applications are managed per file type or protocol in Settings, where the .pdf association can be pointed to a different reader.

q: Through which dialog are environment variables such as PATH edited?
options: The Startup tab of Task Manager, using the detailed processes view
The Clock and Region settings pages in the Control Panel window
System Properties, on the Advanced tab, using Environment Variables
Windows Security, under the Firewall and network protection page
explain: The Environment Variables dialog, reached from System Properties or the About page in Settings, edits user and system variables including PATH.

q: What symptom suggests that the PATH environment variable has been corrupted?
options: The screen resolution and scaling reset themselves at every user sign-in
Commands that ran from any folder now report that they are not recognized
The computer fails to power on at all when the power button is pressed
Files stored on the system drive suddenly lose all of their permissions
explain: If a tool's folder is removed from PATH, the shell can no longer find that command by name from other directories, producing a 'not recognized' error.

q: Which description best defines virtual memory (the Windows page file)?
options: Disk space Windows uses as overflow when physical RAM is exhausted
A second physical memory module inside the PC
The dedicated memory built into the graphics card
A permanent compressed backup of everything in RAM
explain: The page file lets Windows move less-used memory pages to disk when RAM fills; a page file that is too small causes low-memory errors under load.

q: What does the Windows Search indexing service most affect?
options: Only the total time the computer needs to complete its boot and sign-in sequence
The overall speed and throughput of the computer's wired and wireless connections
How quickly the printer wizard can discover and install new printers on the network
How fast file content and mail items are found, with a rebuild fixing chronic search failures
explain: The indexer catalogs file properties and content so searches return results quickly; a corrupt index is rebuilt from Indexing Options.

q: What is the powercfg command used to manage and report on?
options: Defragmentation schedules for the system disk
The list of local user accounts on the PC
Power settings, including battery health and sleep reports
Formatting options for removable USB drives
explain: Powercfg queries and changes power plans and generates reports such as /batteryreport and /sleepstudy that are standard for laptop troubleshooting.

q: A laptop repeatedly wakes inside a carrying bag and drains its battery. What is a likely cause?
options: A cracked or failing display panel on the laptop's lid assembly
Wake timers or Wake on LAN enabled in the power settings
Too many shortcut icons arranged across the Windows desktop
A Recycle Bin that has not been emptied for several months
explain: Wake timers and network wake features can rouse a sleeping laptop; disabling them in the active power plan stops the phantom wakes.

q: How can an administrator stop Windows from restarting for updates during working hours?
options: By configuring Active Hours and, in managed environments, update policies
By setting disk quotas on the system drive
By changing the user's screen saver timeout
By enabling File History on an external drive
explain: Active Hours tells Windows Update when not to restart automatically, and organizations can enforce restart behavior through policy.

q: After malware cleanup, double-clicking .exe files no longer launches programs. How is this repaired?
options: By formatting the system drive completely and starting over with a fresh install
By reinstalling the device driver package for the computer's monitor and display
By disabling User Account Control permanently in the local security policy settings
By restoring the default .exe file association after confirming the system is clean
explain: Malware frequently hijacks the exefile association; restoring the default registry association values fixes program launching once the infection is gone.

q: Which utility should be opened first to learn why a workstation rebooted unexpectedly overnight?
options: Disk Cleanup, reviewing the size and history of temporary files on the drive
Task Scheduler, reviewing the history and results of overnight scheduled tasks
Event Viewer, checking the System log for Kernel-Power and BugCheck events
The Windows Store, reviewing the history of app updates installed overnight
explain: The System log records unexpected shutdowns as Kernel-Power event 41 and bugcheck events for crashes, which explain a surprise reboot.

q: What does running the winver command display?
options: The Windows product key used for activation
A dialog showing the Windows version and OS build number
The version of the computer's BIOS firmware
A list of the printers installed on the PC
explain: Winver shows the Windows edition, feature version such as 23H2, and OS build number needed for compatibility and support checks.

q: What is the main advantage of Windows Terminal over the legacy console host?
options: Hosts Command Prompt, PowerShell, and WSL shells in tabs within one app
Provides a graphical console for managing services and scheduled tasks
Replaces PowerShell with a new scripting language for automation work
Serves as the default file manager for local and network drives
explain: Windows Terminal is a modern multi-tab host that can run Command Prompt, PowerShell, and WSL distributions side by side in one window.

q: What does the PowerShell execution policy primarily control?
options: How quickly script files are processed by the PowerShell engine
Which user accounts are allowed to open a PowerShell window
Which network locations a cmdlet can contact during a session
Whether script files are allowed to run and what signing they require
explain: Execution policies such as Restricted and RemoteSigned gate whether .ps1 files run and whether they must be signed. They are a safety boundary, not a speed or network setting.

q: A user cannot delete a file because another process has it open. Which tool can identify the process holding the file?
options: Disk Cleanup, using the temporary files report for the volume
System Configuration, using the Services tab for the session
Resource Monitor, using the Associated Handles search on the CPU tab
Reliability Monitor, using the problem history report for the day
explain: Searching for the file name under Associated Handles in Resource Monitor shows the process that has a handle to it, so that process can be closed first.

q: What does the Triggers tab define for a scheduled task in Task Scheduler?
options: Which user account the task uses when it accesses the network
When or on what event the task runs, such as a time or a logon
What priority the task receives compared with other running tasks
Where the task file is stored in the Task Scheduler library
explain: Triggers start a task by time or by event such as logon or idle. Actions define what the task runs, while Conditions and Settings refine its behavior.

q: A scheduled task must run at night even when no one is signed in. Which setting must be selected for that to happen?
options: Run whether the user is logged on or not, storing credentials as needed
Run with highest privileges, without changing any sign-in setting
Use a weekly trigger, without changing any sign-in setting
Show the task as hidden, without changing any sign-in setting
explain: Unattended tasks need the option to run whether the user is logged on or not, so the task can run under stored credentials when no session exists.

q: A technician suspects errors on the Windows system volume and wants a disk check scheduled for the next restart. Which action does that?
options: Running Disk Cleanup and selecting the system files option for the volume
Running Optimize Drives and selecting the system volume for analysis
Opening Task Manager and selecting the system process for the volume
Running chkdsk with the fix option on the in-use system volume
explain: The system volume cannot be locked while Windows is running, so chkdsk offers to schedule the check for the next boot instead.

q: On which Windows edition is the Local Group Policy Editor unavailable by default?
options: Windows Pro, when installed on a domain-joined workstation
Windows Enterprise, when installed on a managed workstation
Windows Home, when installed on a personal workstation
Windows Education, when installed on a school workstation
explain: gpedit.msc is included with Pro, Education, and Enterprise editions. Windows Home does not include the editor by default.

q: An administrator needs local policies that apply to one specific user instead of to every user on a PC. Which approach should the administrator use?
options: A separate policy created in the Disk Management console for that user
A multiple local Group Policy setup in an MMC snap-in for that user
A second user profile created in the Settings app for that user
A custom desktop created in the Task View panel for that user
explain: Multiple Local Group Policy lets an administrator build a user-specific local policy console in MMC, separate from the policy that applies to all users.

q: What does the Clean up system files option in Disk Cleanup add the ability to remove?
options: Old Windows update files and files from a previous Windows installation
Personal documents that have not been opened for a long period
Printer drivers that are currently in use by connected printers
Active restore points that Windows created during the last update
explain: With elevation, Disk Cleanup can remove update caches and the previous installation in Windows.old, which often reclaims many gigabytes after an upgrade.

q: What does Storage Sense automate on a Windows PC that is running low on space?
options: Backing up personal folders to OneDrive on a recurring schedule
Optimizing solid-state drives when fragmentation is detected
Scanning local drives for malware when threats are detected
Freeing space by clearing temporary files, old downloads, and Recycle Bin contents
explain: Storage Sense is the built-in housekeeping feature that automatically clears temporary files, aged downloads, and Recycle Bin contents on a schedule.

q: What happens when a user chooses Reset this PC with the cloud download option?
options: All installed desktop apps are kept exactly as they were before
A DVD or USB installer is required before the reset can begin
A fresh Windows image is downloaded from Microsoft for the reset
The reset becomes available only on PCs joined to a domain
explain: Cloud download fetches a clean Windows image from Microsoft instead of reusing local recovery files, which helps when those local files are damaged.

q: What can a user do from the Startup Settings menu that is reached through the Windows Recovery Environment?
options: Change the firmware password that protects the BIOS settings screen
Boot Safe Mode variants or disable driver signature enforcement for one boot
Raise the processor clock speed for faster troubleshooting sessions
Reformat the recovery partition to create additional free space
explain: Startup Settings offers one-time boot choices such as Safe Mode, disabling driver signature enforcement, and disabling early-launch anti-malware.

q: Which method can remove a driver package from the Windows driver store?
options: Using pnputil with the delete-driver option for the package
Using ipconfig with the release option for the package
Using the Photos app to manage the package in the store
Using Disk Cleanup alone to manage the package in the store
explain: pnputil manages packages in the driver store, and Device Manager can also delete the driver when uninstalling a device. Removing stale packages can resolve driver conflicts.

q: Which pair of commands releases a DHCP lease and then requests a new one on a Windows host?
options: ipconfig /flushdns followed by ipconfig /registerdns in sequence
ipconfig /release followed by ipconfig /renew in sequence
ipconfig /all followed by ipconfig /displaydns in sequence
ipconfig /showclassid followed by ipconfig /setclassid in sequence
explain: The release command drops the current lease and the renew command requests a new assignment from DHCP. Flushing DNS only clears the resolver cache.

q: A technician needs the MAC address, DHCP server, and lease times for a Windows host. Which command shows that full configuration?
options: ipconfig /all, which lists adapters with physical and DHCP details
ipconfig, which lists adapters with physical and DHCP details
netstat /all, which lists adapters with physical and DHCP details
arp /all, which lists adapters with physical and DHCP details
explain: The /all switch extends ipconfig to show physical addresses, DHCP and DNS servers, and lease information for each adapter.

q: Websites fail when opened by name but work when opened by IP address, and the DNS server settings are correct. Which command should the technician try next?
options: ipconfig /release, to request a new address from the DHCP server
chkdsk /f, to check the system volume for file system errors
netstat -ano, to list connections and the owning process IDs
ipconfig /flushdns, to clear the local DNS resolver cache
explain: A stale or poisoned resolver cache can return wrong results for names while IP access still works. Flushing the cache forces fresh resolution.

q: A technician wants the replies from a connectivity test to show hostnames for the target IP addresses. Which command should the technician use?
options: ping -t, which continues testing until the user stops the test manually
ping -n, which sets how many echo requests the test sends in total
ping -a, which resolves target IP addresses to hostnames in the replies
ping -l, which sets the size of the echo request the test sends out
explain: The -a switch performs reverse name resolution for the target. The -t switch pings continuously, -n sets the count, and -l sets the packet size.

q: A technician is checking the path MTU and wants to send large test packets that must not be fragmented. Which command does that?
options: ping -t, which sends requests continuously until it is stopped
ping -f with -l, which sets do-not-fragment and a packet size
tracert -h, which sets the maximum hops searched for a target
pathping -n, which skips resolving addresses for each hop found
explain: Setting the do-not-fragment flag with a chosen size lets the technician find the largest packet that survives the path, which reveals the bottleneck MTU.

q: How does the pathping tool differ from the tracert tool on Windows?
options: It also measures packet loss at each hop over a period of time
It uses only UDP packets where tracert uses only ICMP packets
It works only on IPv6 networks where tracert works only on IPv4
It requires elevation where tracert works only for standard users
explain: Pathping combines a route trace with per-hop packet-loss statistics gathered over time, giving more detail about where loss occurs than tracert alone.

q: Which netstat switch displays the executable involved in each connection?
options: netstat -r
netstat -s
netstat -e
netstat -b
explain: -b shows the creating program (requires elevation); -ano shows PIDs, -r the routing table.

q: What is the main diagnostic purpose of the nslookup command?
options: Listing the open ports and owning processes on a local host
Renewing the DHCP lease and DNS registration on a local host
Querying DNS servers directly to test how names are resolved
Testing the physical quality of a network cable on a local host
explain: nslookup queries a chosen DNS server directly, interactively or with a single command, so a technician can validate specific records and server responses.

q: What is the nbtstat command used to inspect on a Windows host?
options: Bluetooth device pairings and recent connection history for the host
NetBIOS over TCP/IP statistics, name tables, and the name cache
NTFS permissions and access control entries for folders on the host
Battery status and recent power events recorded for the host
explain: nbtstat displays NetBIOS name tables, sessions, and cache information. It is a legacy tool, but it remains part of the A+ objectives.

q: Which command maps a network share to a drive letter on a Windows host?
options: net use, which connects a shared resource to a local drive letter
net share, which connects a shared resource to a local drive letter
net user, which connects a shared resource to a local drive letter
net start, which connects a shared resource to a local drive letter
explain: net use with a drive letter and a UNC path maps the share for the session. By contrast, net share publishes a local folder as a share.

q: Which command lists all currently running processes from the Windows command line?
options: taskkill /list, which enumerates processes with their process IDs
services.msc, which enumerates processes with their process IDs
msinfo32, which enumerates processes with their process IDs
tasklist, which enumerates processes with their process IDs
explain: tasklist lists running processes with PIDs and memory use. taskkill ends processes, using a PID or image name from that list.

q: Which command ends a process by its process ID from the Windows command line?
options: tasklist with a kill switch and the process ID to be ended
shutdown with a process switch and the process ID to be ended
taskkill with the PID switch and the process ID to be ended
net stop with a process switch and the process ID to be ended
explain: taskkill targets a process by PID or image name, and the force switch ends it when a graceful close does not work.

q: What does the command shutdown /r /t 0 do on a Windows PC?
options: Shuts the PC down after a delay of one hour has elapsed
Restarts the PC immediately with no delay before restarting
Signs the current user out without restarting the PC at all
Puts the PC into hibernation without restarting it at all
explain: In the shutdown command, /r requests a restart and /t sets the delay in seconds, so a value of 0 means the restart happens now.

q: Which command checks and repairs protected Windows system files using the component store?
options: sfc /scannow, which scans protected files against the component store
chkdsk /scannow, which scans protected files against the component store
defrag /scan, which scans protected files against the component store
diskpart /verify, which scans protected files against the component store
explain: System File Checker scans protected system files and replaces corrupt copies with good copies from the component store.

q: System File Checker cannot repair files because the component store itself is corrupt. Which step should be taken before running it again?
options: Formatting the system drive and reinstalling Windows from media
Disabling Windows Update so the store stops changing its files
Deleting the WinSxS folder so Windows rebuilds it from scratch
Running DISM with RestoreHealth, then running System File Checker again
explain: DISM can repair the component store, using Windows Update as a source, so that System File Checker has good copies available to restore from.

q: How does the /r switch for chkdsk differ from the /f switch?
options: It only checks file names, without checking the file system structure
It completes more quickly, without checking the file system structure
It also locates bad sectors and recovers readable information from them
It checks only removable drives, without checking internal drives at all
explain: The /r switch adds a surface scan for bad sectors and recovery of readable data, and it implies /f. That extra scan makes it take much longer.

q: In diskpart, which command sequence removes a selected disk's partition table entirely?
options: Formatting the disk with a quick NTFS format from diskpart
Selecting the disk, then running the clean command in diskpart
Deleting one partition with the override switch from diskpart
Clearing the disk attributes with the attributes command in diskpart
explain: After a disk is selected, the clean command removes all partitioning information from it. It is destructive, so the selected disk must be verified first.

q: Which command-line tool is preferred for scripted backups because it can copy security settings, retry failed files, and mirror a folder tree?
options: robocopy, which supports mirroring, security copying, retries, and logging
copy, which supports mirroring, security copying, retries, and logging
move, which supports mirroring, security copying, retries, and logging
xcopy, which supports mirroring, security copying, retries, and logging
explain: Robocopy, or Robust File Copy, is built for scripted copying with mirroring, security settings, retry logic, multi-threading, and detailed logging.

q: What is the major risk of running a robocopy job with the mirror switch?
options: All copied files are compressed in the destination by default
The computer must be restarted before the copied files can be used
File permissions in the destination are randomized during the job
Files deleted from the source are also deleted from the destination
explain: Mirroring makes the destination match the source exactly, so deletions in the source propagate to the destination. Pointing a mirror job at the wrong source can erase a backup.

q: What is the attrib command used to view or change on a Windows file?
options: The drive letter that is assigned to the volume holding the file
The NTFS permissions that are assigned to users for the file
File attributes such as read-only, hidden, system, and archive flags
EFS encryption settings that are assigned to users for the file
explain: attrib displays and changes attribute flags such as read-only and hidden. NTFS permissions are managed separately, for example with icacls.

q: What does the command gpresult /r display for the signed-in user?
options: All registry keys that were changed during the last policy refresh
The Resultant Set of Policy applied to the user and the computer
The list of services that are currently running on the computer
Recent file changes that were made since the last policy refresh
explain: gpresult reports which Group Policy objects applied and what settings resulted. The /h switch produces the same information as an HTML report.

q: Which command forces an immediate Group Policy refresh, including computer policies?
options: gpupdate /force, which reapplies user and computer policy immediately
gpedit /refresh, which reapplies user and computer policy immediately
ipconfig /renew, which reapplies user and computer policy immediately
net start policy, which reapplies user and computer policy immediately
explain: gpupdate reapplies Group Policy without waiting for the background refresh interval, and /force reapplies settings even if they appear unchanged.

q: What does running whoami with the groups switch reveal about the current sign-in?
options: The IP configuration assigned to the computer during sign-in
All local user accounts that exist on the computer itself
The serial number reported by the computer BIOS at startup
The security groups present in the current access token, with their SIDs
explain: whoami /groups lists the group memberships and SIDs actually present in the logon token, which confirms whether a group change has taken effect.

q: What does the driverquery command list on a Windows PC?
options: Driver files that were recently moved to the Recycle Bin
Unsigned drivers that were blocked during the last startup
All installed device drivers together with their current status
Printer queues that are currently paused on the local PC
explain: driverquery produces an inventory of installed drivers and their status, and its signature switch can flag signing information for each driver.

q: When is the bootrec /rebuildbcd command used during Windows startup repair?
options: When the partition table on the system disk uses the GPT style
When the Boot Configuration Data store is missing Windows installations
When Windows starts normally and no boot repair is being performed
When a user needs a forgotten sign-in password to be recovered
explain: RebuildBCD scans the disks for Windows installations and offers to add missing entries to the Boot Configuration Data store during startup repair.

q: What is the bcdedit tool used to view and change on a Windows PC?
options: Boot Configuration Data entries such as the default OS and timeout
BIOS setup options such as the boot password and fan settings
The format and layout of the EFI partition on the system disk
Local user accounts such as the default account and guest account
explain: bcdedit edits the Boot Configuration Data store that the boot manager reads, such as default entry and menu timeout. Changes take effect at the next boot.

q: Which command rewrites a corrupted Master Boot Record on a legacy BIOS system from the Recovery Environment?
options: bootrec /fixboot, which writes a new boot sector to the system partition
diskpart clean, which removes all partitions from the system disk entirely
sfc /fixmbr, which scans system files on the system disk entirely
bootrec /fixmbr, which writes a fresh Master Boot Record to the disk
explain: The /fixmbr switch writes a fresh Master Boot Record, while /fixboot writes a new boot sector. Both are used from the Windows Recovery Environment.

q: What does adding the quick switch to the format command do during formatting?
options: Performs a factory low-level format that rewrites every track
Performs a secure multi-pass wipe that overwrites every sector
Performs a quick format that skips scanning for bad sectors
Performs a partition resize that keeps the existing file system
explain: A quick format reinitializes the file system without scanning every sector. A full format checks the surface and, on modern Windows, overwrites the data.

q: Which PowerShell cmdlet can test connectivity to a specific host and TCP port when ping may be blocked?
options: Get-Ping, using the target host and port number for the test
Test-NetConnection, using the target host and port number for the test
Invoke-WebRequest, using the target host and port number for the test
Trace-Route, using the target host and port number for the test
explain: Test-NetConnection can check a specific TCP port, such as 443, so it can succeed where ICMP ping is filtered by a firewall.

q: The PowerShell cmdlets Get-Service, Start-Service, and Stop-Service manage the same objects as which GUI tool?
options: The Services console, which lists and controls Windows services
The Processes tab, which lists and controls running applications
Disk Management, which lists and controls volumes and partitions
Event Viewer, which lists and controls Windows event log entries
explain: The service cmdlets start, stop, and report on the same Windows services that are shown in the Services console, services.msc.

q: What are the PowerShell cmdlets Get-EventLog and Get-WinEvent used to do?
options: Clear the paging file when the system drive is low on space
List the printers that are installed for the current user
Edit registry values that control how event logging works
Read Windows event logs from the shell for filtering and scripting
explain: Get-WinEvent queries event logs with filters, which makes it useful for automated log review and troubleshooting scripts.

q: The PowerShell cmdlets Get-NetIPAddress and Get-NetAdapter largely replace which legacy tools for viewing adapter configuration?
options: Defragment and Optimize Drives and the Disk Cleanup utility
Notepad and the Windows Accessories folder on the Start menu
ipconfig and the Network Connections graphical interface
Paint and the Windows Accessories folder on the Start menu
explain: The NetTCPIP and NetAdapter modules expose IP and adapter configuration as PowerShell objects, covering much of what ipconfig and the GUI previously showed.

q: How can a technician run a downloaded PowerShell script for one session only, without permanently changing the execution policy?
options: Formatting the drive and reinstalling PowerShell for that session only
Setting the execution policy to Bypass for the Process scope only
Disabling antivirus protection permanently for that session only
Deleting the policy registry keys for that session only entirely
explain: Setting the policy at Process scope changes it only for the current PowerShell session, which is the standard way to run a one-off script without a lasting change.

q: Which Linux command shows running processes in an interactive display that updates continuously?
options: top, which updates process and resource use in real time
ps -list, which updates process and resource use in real time
procmon, which updates process and resource use in real time
taskmgr, which updates process and resource use in real time
explain: top shows live process and resource usage and updates continuously. The ps command gives a static snapshot at the moment it runs.

q: What does the Linux command ps aux show on a system?
options: Only the processes belonging to the current user's shell session
Available disk space for the file systems mounted on the system
Users who are currently signed in to sessions on the system
All processes on the system, with user, CPU, and memory details
explain: The BSD-style aux options list every process on the system with owner and resource columns such as CPU and memory use.

q: What happens when a Linux process receives the signal sent by kill -9?
options: It receives SIGTERM and is asked to shut down gracefully
It receives a signal that restarts the whole Linux system
It receives SIGKILL and ends immediately without any cleanup
It receives a signal that pauses it until it is resumed later
explain: Signal 9 is SIGKILL, which cannot be caught or ignored, so the process ends at once. Signal 15, SIGTERM, is the graceful default request.

q: What does the Linux command systemctl status sshd display?
options: Disk usage for the configuration directory used by the system
The state and recent log lines of the SSH service unit itself
All network connections that are currently open on the system
The version of the kernel that is currently running on the system
explain: systemctl manages systemd units, and the status form shows whether a unit such as sshd is active along with its most recent log lines.

q: Which Linux command makes a service start automatically when the system boots?
options: systemctl enable, which creates the boot-time links for the service
systemctl start, which creates the boot-time links for the service
service --boot, which creates the boot-time links for the service
chmod +x, which creates the boot-time links for the service file
explain: Enabling a unit creates the links systemd uses at boot. Starting a unit only runs it in the current session and does not enable it.

q: What does the Linux command df -h report about a system?
options: The sizes of individual directories in human-readable form
The amount of free memory in human-readable form for use
The handles of files that are currently open on the system
Disk space usage of mounted file systems in human-readable sizes
explain: df reports capacity and usage for mounted file systems, and -h presents the sizes in readable units. Directory sizes are reported by du instead.

q: What does the Linux command free -h display about a system?
options: Partitions and file systems that are mounted on the system
The temperature of the processor that is installed in the system
RAM and swap usage in a human-readable summary for the system
Network throughput for the adapters that are active on the system
explain: free reports total, used, and available memory along with swap usage, and -h presents those values in readable units.

q: Which Linux command shows new lines at the end of a growing log file in real time?
options: cat with a watch option, following new lines as they are written
tail -f, following new lines at the end of the file as written
head -f, following new lines at the end of the file as written
less with a stream option, following new lines as they are written
explain: The follow option for tail keeps the file open and prints lines as they are appended. journalctl -f does the same for the systemd journal.

q: What is the Linux command journalctl -u followed by a unit name used to do?
options: Read the systemd journal entries recorded for that specific service
Edit the unit file that controls how that specific service runs
List the user accounts that can administer that specific service
Check the disk health reported for that specific service unit
explain: journalctl can filter the systemd journal by unit, time, or priority, which makes it a primary tool for reviewing a service's logs.

q: What does the macOS Terminal command diskutil list show?
options: Only the external drives that are currently connected to the Mac
Processes that are currently running in the background on the Mac
Wi-Fi networks that are currently available around the Mac
All disks, partitions, and volumes that are known to the Mac
explain: diskutil is the macOS disk management command-line tool, and its list form enumerates devices, partitions, and APFS containers and volumes.

q: What is Homebrew in the context of macOS administration?
options: An official Apple utility for browsing the Mac App Store catalog
An official Apple utility for backing up a Mac to external media
A third-party package manager for installing command-line tools and apps
A third-party platform for running virtual machines on a Mac
explain: Homebrew, invoked as brew, installs and updates packages from the shell on macOS and Linux. It is not an Apple App Store tool.

q: Which keyboard shortcut opens the crosh shell on ChromeOS?
options: Ctrl+Shift+Esc, pressed together on the ChromeOS keyboard
Ctrl+Alt+T, pressed together on the ChromeOS keyboard
Alt+F4, pressed together on the ChromeOS keyboard
Ctrl+Alt+Delete, pressed together on the ChromeOS keyboard
explain: Ctrl+Alt+T opens crosh, which provides basic diagnostics. A fuller Linux shell comes from the Linux environment on ChromeOS or from developer mode.

q: A folder is accessed over the network and both NTFS permissions and share permissions apply. What is the effective permission for that access?
options: The NTFS permission alone, ignoring the share permission entirely
The share permission alone, ignoring the NTFS permission entirely
The most restrictive of the two permissions that apply to the access
The combined total of both permissions that apply to the access
explain: Network access must pass both the share layer and the NTFS layer, so the effective result is whichever permission is more restrictive.

q: How does an explicit Deny entry in NTFS permissions generally affect access?
options: It is ignored whenever any Allow entry exists for that permission
It overrides any Allow entry that exists for that same permission
It applies to files on the volume but never to folders on it
It applies to standard users on the volume but never to administrators
explain: Deny entries take precedence over Allow entries in a Windows access check, and an explicit deny is the strongest form of that rule.

q: A user MOVES a file from one NTFS folder to another folder on the SAME volume. What happens to its permissions?
options: The file keeps its original permissions
It inherits the destination folder's permissions
Permissions are reset to defaults
Permissions are lost entirely
explain: Moving within the same volume only relocates the file's directory entry, so its ACL travels with it. Copying (or moving across volumes) creates a new file that inherits the destination folder's permissions.

q: A file is copied to a different NTFS folder on the same PC. What happens to its permissions?
options: They stay exactly as they were in the source folder for the file
They become Full Control for Everyone in the destination folder
They are removed so the copied file has no permissions at all
They are inherited from the new destination folder for the file
explain: A copy creates a new file, so it takes the inheritable permissions of the destination folder instead of keeping the source file's permissions.

q: At what level does the Encrypting File System protect files on Windows?
options: At the whole-disk level, covering every file on the volume equally
At the network-share level, covering every file in the share equally
At the individual file and folder level, transparently for each user
At the firmware level, covering every file before Windows starts
explain: EFS encrypts individual files and folders using keys tied to a user account. BitLocker, by contrast, protects the whole volume.

q: A user encrypted files with EFS, and the user profile and keys are lost with no recovery agent or backed-up certificate. What is the result?
options: Windows decrypts the files automatically at the next system startup
The encrypted data is effectively unrecoverable without the key
Any administrator account can read the files without the key
The encrypted files are converted to an archive format for recovery
explain: Without the private key or a designated recovery agent, EFS-encrypted data cannot be decrypted, which is why backing up the certificate is essential.

q: How do NTFS compression and EFS encryption interact when both are applied to the same file?
options: They are mutually exclusive; a file can use one but not both together
They are always applied together whenever either one is selected
They are available together only when the volume uses the FAT32 system
They are applied by default together to every file on the volume
explain: Windows does not allow a file to be both NTFS-compressed and EFS-encrypted at the same time, so selecting one removes the other.

q: Which NTFS permission lets a user read, write, change, and delete files, but not change permissions or take ownership?
options: Full Control, which also allows changing permissions and taking ownership
Write only, which also allows changing permissions and taking ownership
List folder contents, which also allows changing permissions and taking ownership
Modify, which allows the file work but not changing permissions or ownership
explain: The permission described allows reading, writing, changing, and deleting content, while Full Control is the level that adds changing permissions and taking ownership.

q: An administrator needs a record of who has been accessing a sensitive file. Which steps must be taken first?
options: Installing a third-party monitoring tool and reviewing its console daily
Enabling File History and reviewing the versions it saves for the file
Enabling Audit Object Access, setting auditing on the file, and checking the Security log
Enabling Storage Sense and reviewing the space it frees for the file
explain: Auditing takes two steps: the policy enables the object-access category, and the file's auditing entries define which attempts to record in the Security log.

q: On an NTFS volume, disk quotas are tracked on what basis?
options: Per folder, based on the folders a user stores files inside
Per user, for each volume on which quotas are configured
Per file type, based on the extensions a user stores most
Per computer, based on the machine that hosts the volume
explain: Quota entries are maintained for each user on each volume, and enforcement can deny further writes once a user's limit is exceeded.

q: What does converting a basic disk to a dynamic disk in Disk Management enable?
options: Software volumes that can span multiple disks in Windows
GPT partitioning for disks that use the newer partition style
BitLocker encryption for volumes that need whole-drive protection
Faster SATA transfers for disks that support higher link speeds
explain: Dynamic disks support multi-disk volumes managed by Windows, such as spanned, striped, and mirrored volumes, a role now largely taken by Storage Spaces.

q: What does a mirrored volume in Disk Management or Storage Spaces provide?
options: Double usable capacity with no additional risk to stored data
Striping for performance only, with no duplication of stored data
Automatic backup of stored data to a cloud storage account
Fault tolerance by duplicating data across two separate drives
explain: A mirrored layout keeps an exact copy of the data on a second drive, so the volume can survive the failure of one drive.

q: A parity layout in Storage Spaces is most comparable to which traditional arrangement?
options: RAID 0 striping, which spreads data without any redundancy at all
A single backup file, which stores one copy of selected data only
RAID 5, which is capacity-efficient with single-drive fault tolerance
JBOD with checksums only, which stores data without any redundancy
explain: Parity spaces stripe data together with parity information, surviving one drive failure while using less overhead than mirroring, at some write cost.

q: Extending a volume in Disk Management fails because there is no adjacent unallocated space. What is a common workaround?
options: Defragmenting the drive so the free space moves next to the volume
Backing up, deleting, and recreating the partition layout as needed
Disabling the paging file permanently so the volume can be extended
Converting the disk to FAT32 so the volume can be extended freely
explain: Windows can extend a volume only into contiguous unallocated space immediately after it, so the layout often must be rebuilt or adjusted with another tool.

q: Volumes formatted with the Resilient File System are most associated with which use?
options: Servers and Storage Spaces deployments that need high resilience
Boot drives for standard Windows 11 desktop installations at home
USB flash drives used for transferring files between computers
Optical media used for distributing software installation files
explain: ReFS is designed for data volumes and server deployments with integrity features that reduce the need for chkdsk. Windows still boots from NTFS.

q: How does a full format differ from a quick format of a volume?
options: It always completes faster than a quick format of the same volume
It keeps the old file table so files can be recovered more easily
It changes only the volume label and leaves the file system as is
It scans the whole volume for bad sectors and overwrites the data
explain: A full format checks the entire surface and, on modern Windows, zeroes the data. A quick format only reinitializes the file system metadata.

q: What is the maximum size of a single file that can be stored on a FAT32 volume?
options: 2 GB, which is the largest single file FAT32 can store in total
16 GB, which is the largest single file FAT32 can store in total
4 GB minus one byte, which is the largest single file FAT32 can store
Unlimited, because FAT32 places no limit on a single file's size
explain: FAT32 cannot store a file that reaches 4 GB, which is the classic reason large-file copies to FAT32 USB drives fail near that size.

q: What was the exFAT file system designed primarily for?
options: System boot volumes that need advanced security and journaling features
Flash storage that needs large-file support without NTFS overhead
Floppy disks that need backward compatibility with older systems
Network shares that need centralized permissions and auditing features
explain: exFAT removes the FAT32 file-size limit for removable flash media such as USB drives and SD cards while staying lighter than NTFS.

q: Which file system does macOS use on modern internal drives?
options: APFS, which is optimized for solid-state storage on Apple devices
HFS+ only, which is optimized for solid-state storage on Apple devices
NTFS, which is optimized for solid-state storage on Apple devices
ext4, which is optimized for solid-state storage on Apple devices
explain: APFS is Apple's current file system, designed for SSDs with features such as snapshots, cloning, and strong encryption support.

q: What is the standard native file system on most Linux distributions today?
options: NTFS, which is the default journaling file system for most distributions
APFS, which is the default journaling file system for most distributions
ReFS, which is the default journaling file system for most distributions
ext4, which is the default journaling file system for most distributions
explain: ext4 is the default journaling file system for most Linux distributions, although some distributions use XFS or Btrfs instead.

q: How does defragmenting a traditional hard drive improve its performance?
options: It increases the total capacity available for storing files on the drive
It repairs bad sectors that have been detected across the drive surface
It reassembles file fragments contiguously so reads need less head movement
It encrypts stored data so reads can be verified across the drive surface
explain: Fragmented files force a spinning disk's head to seek repeatedly. Defragmentation restores a more sequential layout so reads are faster.

q: Why does Windows run TRIM optimization instead of defragmentation on solid-state drives?
options: Solid-state drives complete defragmentation too quickly to be useful at all
Defragmentation gives no benefit on flash and shortens drive life with extra writes
TRIM removes user files from solid-state drives to create additional space
Defragmentation is prohibited on solid-state drives by the drive firmware itself
explain: SSDs have no seek penalty, so defragmentation does not help performance. TRIM tells the drive which blocks are free so garbage collection stays efficient.

q: What do shadow copies, shown as Previous Versions, allow users to do?
options: Restore earlier versions of files and folders from automatic snapshots
Run a second copy of Windows alongside the current installation
Hide selected files and folders from administrator accounts entirely
Extend disk quotas for users who have reached their assigned limit
explain: Volume Shadow Copy snapshots power the Previous Versions feature, letting users recover earlier versions of files without a full restore.

q: What happens when a mapped drive is created with net use and the persistent switch set to yes?
options: The mapping becomes visible to every user account on the computer
The mapping stays connected even when the network is unavailable
The mapping forces the connection to use the SMBv1 protocol always
The mapping reconnects automatically at each subsequent sign-in
explain: Persistent mappings are saved and restored at sign-in. Non-persistent mappings last only for the current session.

q: What is the administrative share that appears as C$ on a Windows PC?
options: A public share of the drive that is available to every network user
A share of the optical drive that is available to every network user
A hidden share of the drive root that is accessible only to administrators
A printer share that is available to every user on the local network
explain: Administrative shares such as C$ and ADMIN$ exist by default for administration, require administrator access, and do not appear when browsing the network.

q: Which of the following is the correct form of a UNC path?
options: server://share/folder, using forward slashes after the server name
\\server\share\folder, using backslashes before the server name
C:\server\share, using a local drive letter before the server name
http://server/share, using a web address before the share name
explain: A UNC path addresses a network resource as two backslashes, the server name, the share name, and then any folders below the share.

q: What is Offline Files, also called Client-Side Caching, designed to do?
options: Keep cached copies of network files available while disconnected, then sync later
Back up an entire file server to a local drive while disconnected overnight
Replace mapped drives with a web interface while disconnected from the network
Block remote access to network files while disconnected from the network
explain: Client-Side Caching lets laptop users keep working with share contents off the network and reconcile changes when they reconnect.

q: A user's whole Windows drive is encrypted with BitLocker. Where should the recovery key be stored?
options: In a text file stored on the same encrypted drive for convenience
Only in the TPM chip, with no other copy kept anywhere else
On a note attached to the monitor in the user's work area
In Active Directory, a Microsoft account, or a separate printed or USB copy
explain: The 48-digit recovery key must be retrievable from somewhere other than the locked disk itself, such as directory services, a Microsoft account, or separate media.

q: Why is enabling Compress this drive on a busy Windows system drive generally discouraged?
options: It removes system files that Windows needs during the startup process
It prevents Windows Update from installing patches on the system drive
It adds processor overhead to every file operation, slowing the system
It reformats the drive before compression can be applied to its files
explain: Whole-drive NTFS compression trades processor work for space on every read and write, which is rarely worthwhile on an operating system volume.

q: Why does ownership of a file matter in the advanced security settings?
options: The owner can always read the file contents, even when it is encrypted
The owner can always change the file's permissions, even if the ACL grants none
The owner can always delete any other file stored on the same volume
The owner can always bypass the disk quotas configured for the volume
explain: A file's owner retains the ability to change its discretionary access control list, which is how administrators regain control by taking ownership.

q: What is lost when a file is moved from an NTFS volume to a FAT32 USB drive?
options: Its NTFS permissions and alternate data streams, which FAT cannot store
Its file name, which must be recreated after the move to the drive
Its contents, which must be recreated after the move to the drive
Its extension, which must be recreated after the move to the drive
explain: FAT32 has no support for NTFS access control lists or alternate data streams, so those elements are dropped when a file is moved to it.

q: Disk Management shows a disk moved from another Windows PC as Foreign. Which action brings its volumes online correctly?
options: Formatting the disk so its volumes can be created again from scratch
Initializing the disk so its volumes can be created again from scratch
Deleting the volumes so the disk can be partitioned again from scratch
Importing the foreign disks so its dynamic volumes come online intact
explain: Dynamic disks moved from another machine appear as Foreign. Importing them preserves their volumes, while initializing the disk would erase them.

q: In which situation is a GPT disk required instead of an MBR disk?
options: When any Linux distribution is installed on the computer's drive
When a USB drive is used for transferring files between computers
When Windows boots in UEFI mode, or when the drive is larger than 2 TB
When a volume on the drive is formatted with the FAT32 file system
explain: MBR is limited to about 2 TB and four primary partitions, and a Windows installation that boots in UEFI mode requires a GPT disk.

q: What does the EFI System Partition contain on a UEFI system?
options: User profiles that were created during the Windows installation process
Boot loaders and boot applications that the UEFI firmware launches
The paging file that Windows creates during the installation process
Printer drivers that were installed during the Windows installation process
explain: UEFI firmware loads boot entries such as Windows Boot Manager from the FAT32 EFI System Partition.

q: What is the main cost of the performance benefit of extending data across a striped volume?
options: Higher failure risk, because losing any member disk loses the whole volume
Half the usable capacity, because every file is stored twice in the volume
Slower single-file reads, because files are stored twice in the volume
A domain controller requirement, because the volume must be managed centrally
explain: Striping spreads data across the member disks for speed, so the failure of any one disk destroys the data for the whole set.

q: Which OS-native source can show which files a departing employee accessed, if the needed setting was enabled beforehand?
options: The Recycle Bin, which records each file the employee opened previously
Task Manager history, which records each file the employee opened previously
Disk Cleanup logs, which record each file the employee opened previously
The Security event log, provided object-access auditing was enabled beforehand
explain: Windows keeps no per-file access history unless object-access auditing was enabled in advance. When it was, the records appear in the Security log.

q: What does Folder Redirection do in a domain environment?
options: Moves all installed programs from workstations to a central server location
Moves the Windows folder from workstations to a central server location
Moves known folders such as Documents and Desktop to a server location
Moves local user profiles from workstations to a cloud storage location
explain: Folder Redirection stores known folders on a server while they still appear local to the user, centralizing the data for backup and management.

q: A user's profile fails to load and Windows signs the user in with a temporary profile. What is a common fix?
options: Reinstalling the printer driver that is assigned to the affected user
Repairing or recreating the user profile after backing up its data first
Increasing the size of the paging file configured for the affected user
Disabling the firewall profile that is assigned to the affected user
explain: Temporary profiles usually result from profile corruption or a locked backup registry entry. Backing up the data and recreating the profile resolves it.

q: What does the NTUSER.DAT file in a user profile store?
options: That user's registry hive, which loads as HKEY_CURRENT_USER at sign-in
That user's documents, which load as the Documents folder at sign-in
That user's email store, which loads as the mailbox file at sign-in
That user's wallpaper image, which loads as the desktop at sign-in
explain: Each profile's NTUSER.DAT becomes the user's HKEY_CURRENT_USER hive at sign-in, so corruption in that file breaks the user's settings.

q: How does a roaming profile differ from a local profile in a domain?
options: It can be used without a password when the user signs in at a PC
It loads only when the computer is started in Safe Mode by the user
It includes the Windows folder when the user signs in at a PC
It is stored on a server and follows the user between domain computers
explain: Roaming profiles are stored on a network share and copy down at sign-in and back at sign-out, so settings follow the user between PCs.

q: When are mandatory profiles most appropriately used for domain users?
options: When users need local administrator rights on the computers they use
When computers must operate without any connection to the network
When users must get an identical desktop whose changes are discarded at sign-out
When only one user account exists on the computers in the environment
explain: Mandatory profiles enforce a fixed, non-persistent environment, which is common for labs and kiosks where changes should not persist.

q: In the standard Linux file system layout, where do user home directories live?
options: In the /etc directory, alongside the system configuration files
In the /home directory, with a subfolder for each standard user
In the /var directory, alongside the system log and spool files
In the /usr/bin directory, alongside the system program files
explain: Standard users each receive a home directory under /home named for the account, while the root account's home is /root.

q: On a Linux system, what permissions does the command chmod 750 grant on a file?
options: Owner: read, write, execute; group: read, execute; others: no access
Owner: full access; group: full access; others: full access to the file
Owner: read only; group: read, write, execute; others: read access
Owner: read, write, execute; group: no access; others: read access
explain: Each octal digit sums read (4), write (2), and execute (1) for one class, so 7 is rwx for the owner, 5 is r-x for the group, and 0 is no access for others.

q: What does the Linux chown command change for a file?
options: The permission bits that control reading, writing, and executing the file
The contents that are stored inside the file on the Linux system
The name that is used to reference the file on the Linux system
The owner and group that are assigned to the file on the system
explain: chown changes ownership of a file, including its user owner and group. chmod changes permission bits, and umask sets defaults for new files.

q: How does Time Machine back up a Mac on modern versions of macOS?
options: It creates a full disk clone every hour as the only backup method used
It creates zip archives of the home folder as the only backup method used
It uses APFS snapshots locally plus incremental backups to the destination disk
It creates FAT32 disk images as the only backup method used for the Mac
explain: Modern Time Machine uses APFS snapshots for local snapshots and keeps incremental versions on the destination, organized by hour, day, and week.

q: How does a standard user account differ from an administrator account on Windows?
options: A standard user cannot run any applications installed on the computer
A standard user cannot save files inside the user's own profile folder
A standard user cannot connect the computer to a Wi-Fi network at all
A standard user cannot install software for all users without elevation credentials
explain: Standard users work within their own scope. Installing software for all users or changing system-wide settings requires administrator credentials through UAC.

q: Which requirement must be met before a PC can be joined to a Windows domain?
options: The signed-in user must hold a Microsoft account with a payment method
The PC must be formatted before it can contact a domain controller
The PC must run Pro, Enterprise, or Education and reach a domain controller
The PC must contain two hard drives before it can join the domain
explain: Windows Home cannot join a domain. The PC must run a business edition, resolve the domain through DNS, and reach a domain controller.

q: A workstation reports that the trust relationship with the primary domain failed after a network change. What is the most likely cause and fix?
options: Cause: the display slept; Fix: restarting the domain controller restores trust
Cause: the machine account password is out of sync; Fix: reset it or rejoin the domain
Cause: the user's password expired; Fix: replacing the workstation restores trust
Cause: DNS is confirmed working; Fix: ignoring the error restores trust over time
explain: Workstations authenticate with a machine-account password. When it falls out of sync with Active Directory, trust fails until the account is reset or the PC rejoins.

q: How does a Windows workgroup differ from a Windows domain?
options: It has no central directory; each PC manages its own user accounts
It requires at least two servers to manage its own user accounts
It encrypts all network traffic between PCs by default for security
It prevents PCs from sharing files and printers with each other entirely
explain: A workgroup is peer-to-peer, with each PC keeping its own account database. A domain provides centralized authentication and policy from directory services.

q: What is the logon format user@domain.com an example of?
options: A Security Identifier, which uniquely identifies a security principal in Windows
A Distinguished Name, which uniquely identifies an object in a directory path
A NetBIOS name, which uniquely identifies a computer on a legacy network
A User Principal Name, which uniquely identifies a user for domain sign-in
explain: A User Principal Name looks like an email address and is the modern format used for signing in to a domain.

q: Group Policy objects are applied in which order?
options: OU, Domain, Site, Local
Domain first, then Local
Local, then Site, then Domain, then OU (LSDOU), with the last applied winning conflicts
Alphabetical by GPO name
explain: LSDOU: later (closer) policies override earlier ones for the same setting unless blocked/enforced.

q: What does it mean when a Group Policy object is marked as Enforced?
options: Its settings are applied twice as often as settings in other policies
Its settings cannot be overridden by later policies or blocked by OU admins
Its settings are applied only to users who hold administrator rights
Its settings disable inheritance for every container in the whole domain
explain: An Enforced, or No Override, policy wins conflicts even when a child OU blocks inheritance or a later policy sets a different value.

q: What does enabling Block Inheritance on an organizational unit stop?
options: Group Policy objects from parent containers applying to that OU, except Enforced ones
All policies, including local policies, applying to computers in that OU entirely
Users in that OU from signing in to computers that belong to that OU
Administrators from ever deleting that OU from the directory structure
explain: Block Inheritance filters out policies inherited from parent containers for that OU. Policies marked Enforced still apply by design.

q: When is loopback processing in Group Policy most appropriately used?
options: When policies need to refresh twice as often on portable computers in the domain
When laptop computers need to keep working while away from the domain network
When logon scripts need to run repeatedly until they complete successfully once
When user settings tied to a computer's location, such as a kiosk, should apply to any user
explain: Loopback processing, in merge or replace mode, makes the user settings linked to the computer's OU govern, which is the classic setup for kiosks and shared hosts.

q: What is the default background Group Policy refresh interval for domain workstations?
options: About 5 minutes, with no random offset added to the interval at all
Exactly 24 hours, with no random offset added to the interval at all
About 90 minutes, with a random offset of up to 30 minutes added
Only at sign-in, with no background refresh during the session at all
explain: Domain computers and users refresh Group Policy in the background about every 90 minutes, plus a random offset of up to 30 minutes to spread the load.

q: An account lockout threshold is set to 5 and the lockout duration is set to 30 minutes. What does that mean for sign-in attempts?
options: The password must contain at least 5 characters and change every 30 minutes
After 5 bad attempts the account locks for 30 minutes or until an admin unlocks it
Users may make 30 attempts before the account locks for a period of 5 minutes
The account is permanently deleted after 5 bad attempts have been recorded
explain: Lockout policy locks an account after the set number of failed attempts for the set duration, balancing brute-force resistance against accidental lockouts.

q: Where are minimum password length and complexity requirements configured for a Windows PC?
options: In Password Policy under Account Policies in Group Policy or local security policy
In Disk Management under the properties of the system volume for the PC
In the firmware setup under the security settings for the PC hardware
In Device Manager under the properties of the security device for the PC
explain: Password Policy sits under Account Policies in Group Policy and in local security policy. Fine-grained password policies can target specific groups in a domain.

q: A service account currently uses a password that never expires. What is the recommended way to manage that account instead?
options: Using the administrator's personal password for the service account instead
Using a shared password recorded in a spreadsheet for the service account
Using the domain administrator password for the service account instead
Using a group Managed Service Account so Active Directory rotates its password
explain: A group Managed Service Account lets Active Directory create and rotate a strong password automatically, removing manual service-account password management.

q: What does Local Security Policy, secpol.msc, configure on a single Windows machine?
options: Domain-wide sites and services for an Active Directory forest
DNS zones and records for computers across an entire network
Audit policy, user rights assignment, and security options for that machine
DHCP scopes and address reservations for an entire subnet
explain: Local Security Policy is the local subset of security settings for one machine. Domain-wide security settings are delivered through Group Policy instead.

q: Which audit category must be enabled to record successful and failed sign-in attempts on a Windows PC?
options: Audit Object Access, which records access to files and other secured objects
Audit Logon Events, which records local and network sign-in attempts on the PC
Audit Directory Service Access, which records changes to directory objects
Audit Process Tracking, which records process creation and exit events on the PC
explain: Logon auditing records events such as 4624 for success and 4625 for failure in the Security log, which is a foundation of security monitoring.

q: In what key way is a Windows Hello PIN considered safer than a password?
options: It is tied to that specific device through the TPM and never travels to a server
It is always exactly 20 characters long and never travels to a server at all
It can be used on any computer and never travels to a server at all
It can never be changed and never travels to a server at all by design
explain: A Hello PIN unlocks keys that are bound to the device, so the PIN alone is of no use without physical access to that specific device.

q: When does the Windows Dynamic Lock feature automatically lock a PC?
options: When the screen saver starts after the configured idle period has elapsed
When the battery charge falls to the configured low-battery level set by the user
When a USB storage drive is removed from the computer by the signed-in user
When the user's paired Bluetooth phone moves out of range of the computer
explain: Dynamic Lock uses the Bluetooth signal from a paired phone as a walk-away signal and locks the PC when that signal is lost.

q: How do OEM Windows licenses differ from retail Windows licenses?
options: They expire after one year of use on the original computer hardware
They include free edition upgrades for the life of the original computer
They are tied to the first motherboard and do not transfer to a new PC
They can be installed on an unlimited number of the owner's computers
explain: An OEM license lives with the original hardware it was first activated on. A retail license can be moved between the owner's PCs.

q: How does KMS activation work in a Windows enterprise environment?
options: Each PC contacts Microsoft individually each time it needs to be activated
A KMS host on the network activates clients, which renew every 180 days
A retail key is installed on each PC and validated once by the KMS host
Internet access is required for every PC each time it starts Windows
explain: Key Management Service activates volume clients against a local host. Clients must renew against the host at least every 180 days to stay activated.

q: How does MAK activation differ from KMS activation for Windows?
options: It activates each machine directly with Microsoft using a key with a set activation count
It activates each machine through a local activation server hosted on the network
It activates each machine once during imaging and never needs activation again after that
It activates each machine through a service that is available only for Linux systems
explain: A Multiple Activation Key suits smaller or disconnected environments, because each machine activates directly with Microsoft until the key's count is used.

q: What is the slmgr.vbs script used to manage on a Windows PC?
options: User accounts and group memberships stored on the local computer
Defragmentation settings for the volume that holds the activation files
The firmware password that protects access to the BIOS setup utility
Windows licensing, including viewing activation status and installing keys
explain: The Software License Manager script installs keys, activates Windows, and reports status through switches such as /dli and /xpr.

q: How does a digital license activate Windows on a PC?
options: It stores the product key in a file on the hard drive for setup to read
It requires a product key sticker on the case for setup to read each time
It links the hardware ID to Microsoft's servers for automatic activation
It requires a phone call to Microsoft each time the computer boots up
explain: A digital license activates automatically when the same hardware contacts Microsoft. Linking it to a Microsoft account helps after major hardware changes.

q: How is an in-place upgrade from Windows 10 Home to Windows Pro typically performed?
options: By reinstalling Windows from installation media and restoring all files afterward
By entering a Pro product key in Activation settings or buying the upgrade in the Store
By contacting the internet service provider and requesting an edition change for the PC
By replacing the processor with one that supports the Pro edition of Windows
explain: An edition upgrade is a key change that unlocks the Pro features in place, so files, settings, and installed apps remain as they were.

q: Why do downgrade rights matter to businesses that license Windows?
options: They allow running an earlier Windows version under a newer version's license
They allow using unlicensed copies of Windows legally in a business setting
They allow returning opened software to the seller for a full refund at any time
They allow skipping activation when Windows is installed in a business setting
explain: Certain volume and OEM licenses permit installing a previous Windows version until the organization is ready to migrate, under Microsoft's terms.

q: What eventually happens to an evaluation copy of Windows that is never activated with a full license?
options: It converts automatically to the Home edition when the evaluation period ends
It deletes all user data stored on the computer when the evaluation period ends
It becomes a fully licensed free copy when the evaluation period ends at last
It expires and begins shutting down or nagging until a full license is applied
explain: Evaluation builds have a fixed lifetime, often 180 days. After that period they enforce activation through shutdowns or persistent notices.

q: Which benefit is integrated into Windows when a user signs in with a Microsoft account?
options: A permanent free subscription to Microsoft Office on every Windows device used
Automatic joining of the computer to an Active Directory domain at sign-in
Settings, passwords, and preferences roaming between the user's Windows devices
Unlimited OneDrive storage included by default with every Microsoft account used
explain: Microsoft account sync roams personalization, Wi-Fi details, and saved credentials across the user's Windows PCs.

q: How does OneDrive Files On-Demand save local disk space on a Windows PC?
options: It compresses every synced file into an archive stored in the OneDrive folder
It shows placeholders and downloads each file only when the file is opened
It deletes duplicate files from the OneDrive folder without asking the user first
It stores synced files inside the Recycle Bin until the user opens them again
explain: Online-only files appear in File Explorer as placeholders and are fetched on first use. Files marked to always keep on the device stay stored locally.

q: In File Explorer, what does a cloud icon overlay on a OneDrive file indicate?
options: The file is online-only in OneDrive and has not yet been downloaded
The file is encrypted with a key that is stored only in OneDrive
The file is corrupted and cannot be downloaded from OneDrive at all
The file is a shared printer that is available through OneDrive sync
explain: The cloud badge marks an online-only placeholder file. A green check mark instead indicates that the file is available locally on the device.

q: To harden a PC on a public network and prevent it joining shared media streaming, which network profile should be set?
options: Private, which treats the network as trusted and enables device discovery
Domain-authenticated, which treats the network as trusted for domain devices
Guest, which treats the network as trusted for temporary visiting devices
Public, which applies stricter firewall rules and disables device discovery
explain: The Public profile treats a network as untrusted, so network discovery and sharing stay off by default and firewall rules are stricter.

q: With which network profile do discovery and file sharing work out of the box on Windows?
options: Public, which is intended for untrusted networks such as coffee-shop Wi-Fi
Metered, which is intended for connections with a limited data allowance
Private, which is intended for trusted networks such as a home or office LAN
Airplane mode, which is intended for travel with wireless radios turned off
explain: A Private profile enables the discovery and sharing services that are meant for trusted local networks. A Public profile disables them by default.

q: Where is the Windows option that requires sign-in when the PC wakes from sleep found?
options: In Control Panel, under the mouse and pointer settings for the PC
In Settings, under Accounts and the sign-in options for the PC
In Task Manager, under the startup apps settings for the PC itself
In Device Manager, under the power settings for the PC hardware
explain: Sign-in options centralize the password, PIN, and Windows Hello requirements, including the behavior when the PC wakes from sleep and Dynamic Lock.

q: What does Fast User Switching allow on a shared Windows PC?
options: Multiple users to stay signed in with apps running while another user works
Administrators to sign in to any account without knowing its password at all
The computer to complete its startup process noticeably faster for every user
Files to copy between user profiles noticeably faster for every signed-in user
explain: Switching users keeps the previous sessions alive in memory, which is convenient but uses RAM and risks unsaved work if the PC is shut down.

q: How does Run as administrator differ from Run as different user in Windows?
options: It installs the app permanently, while the other option removes the app entirely
It skips the UAC prompt in all cases, while the other option always shows a prompt
It requires a restart, while the other option signs the current user out completely
It elevates the current user's token, while the other starts the app under another account
explain: Run as administrator elevates, prompting for credentials when needed. Run as different user, shown with Shift and right-click, launches the app under a completely different account.

q: What can Microsoft Family Safety parental controls enforce for child accounts?
options: Monitoring of employees who sign in with domain accounts at work
Firmware passwords that protect computers before Windows starts
Screen time limits, content filters, and activity reports for child accounts
Usage quotas for printers that are shared with child accounts at home
explain: Family Safety manages child Microsoft accounts across Windows, Xbox, and Android with time limits, content filtering, and activity reporting.

q: Which Windows edition is the business baseline that supports domain join, Group Policy, and BitLocker out of the box?
options: Windows Home, which is aimed at consumers using personal computers at home
Windows Pro, which is aimed at small businesses using managed computers
