Windows in S mode, which is aimed at schools using Store-only computers
Windows RT, which was aimed at tablets using ARM-based computer hardware
explain: Windows Pro adds domain join, the Group Policy editor, BitLocker, Remote Desktop hosting, and Hyper-V over the Home edition.

q: On which Windows editions can a PC natively host incoming Remote Desktop sessions?
options: Pro, Enterprise, and Education, while Home can only act as a client
Home only, while the business editions can only act as clients instead
All editions including Home, with no difference in hosting support at all
No editions at all, because hosting is only a paid add-on service
explain: Windows Home includes the Remote Desktop client but cannot accept incoming sessions. Hosting requires Pro, Enterprise, or Education.

q: On which systems is Hyper-V available as a Windows feature?
options: Home editions running on standard consumer hardware at home
32-bit systems running on older consumer hardware at home
ARM phones running on mobile hardware for application testing
Pro, Enterprise, and Education in 64-bit with SLAT support
explain: Hyper-V requires a business or education edition in 64-bit, plus hardware virtualization with second-level address translation.

q: What does Windows in S mode restrict on a PC?
options: The PC to a single user account for the life of the device itself
The PC to Wi-Fi networks only for the life of the device itself
The PC to apps from the Microsoft Store only, for security and performance
The PC to touch input only for the life of the device itself entirely
explain: S mode limits app installation to the Microsoft Store for security and performance. Switching out of S mode is free but cannot be reversed.

q: Which tool gives the fastest one-stop view of a PC's Windows edition, version, and build for a compatibility check?
options: DirectX Diagnostic Tool, which lists display and sound device details for the PC
Settings under System and About, or winver for the version and build details
The Microsoft Store, which lists apps that are installed and available for the PC
Control Panel under Programs, which lists apps installed on the PC in detail
explain: The About page lists the edition, version, build, and system type in one place, and winver shows the version and build directly.

q: By default, how much clock skew will cause Kerberos tickets to be rejected in a Windows domain?
options: Five minutes of skew between the client clock and the domain clock
One hour of skew between the client clock and the domain clock
Twenty-four hours of skew between the client clock and the domain clock
Thirty seconds of skew between the client clock and the domain clock
explain: Domain members synchronize time from the domain hierarchy. Kerberos rejects tickets when the skew exceeds the default tolerance of five minutes.

q: Which changes does a security baseline applied through Group Policy commonly make?
options: It disables Windows Update permanently across all domain computers by default
It disables all USB storage, including keyboards and mice, across all computers
It disables the Security event log across all domain computers by default entirely
It disables SMBv1 and unused legacy name protocols and restricts local admin membership
explain: Baselines remove legacy protocols such as SMBv1, restrict LLMNR and NetBIOS where they are unused, and tighten who holds local administrator rights.

q: A departing employee's account must be preserved for an investigation but must not be usable. What should the administrator do?
options: Delete the account immediately so it cannot be used by anyone in the company
Rename the account for the next hire so it can be reused without delay at all
Disable the account, preserving its SID, group memberships, and audit trail
Reset the account password to a common word that investigators can guess easily
explain: Disabling preserves the account's identity and history for the investigation while preventing sign-in. Deleting the account destroys the SID link to files and logs.

q: What do cached domain credentials allow a laptop user to do?
options: Sign in without ever providing the domain password for the account
Sign in with the domain account while away from the network, within the cached limit
Gain local administrator rights while away from the office network entirely
Join the laptop to a new domain while away from any network connection
explain: Windows caches a verifier for a limited number of recent domain sign-ins, so travel away from the network does not lock the user out of the laptop.

q: For which accounts does a local password reset disk work?
options: Only for that specific local account, and only if the disk was created beforehand
For any domain account, provided the disk was created on the domain controller
For any Microsoft account, provided the disk was created on another Windows PC
For any local account, even if the disk is created after the password is forgotten
explain: A password reset disk is a per-account USB key for a local account and must exist before the password is forgotten. Microsoft accounts are reset online instead.

q: A user forgets a Microsoft account password at the Windows sign-in screen. What should the user do?
options: Reinstall Windows so a new Microsoft account can be created for the computer
Use an administrator's password to sign in to the Microsoft account instead
Wait 30 days for the Microsoft account password to reset itself automatically
Reset the password online from another device, and let the PC update when back online
explain: Cloud account credentials are recovered through Microsoft's online reset flow, not through local tools. The PC picks up the new password when it is online.

q: What are the two fundamental Windows installation types offered by Setup media?
options: Upgrade, which keeps files and apps, and Custom, which is a clean install
Repair, which keeps files and apps, and Restore, which is a clean install
Express, which keeps files and apps, and Advanced, which is a clean install
Online, which keeps files and apps, and Offline, which is a clean install
explain: Setup offers an Upgrade install to preserve the existing environment, or a Custom install for a fresh installation to a chosen partition.

q: What is the most important preparation before performing an in-place Windows upgrade?
options: Defragmenting the drive so the upgrade files are stored contiguously on disk
Disabling the firewall permanently so the upgrade cannot be interrupted at all
Deleting all restore points so the upgrade starts with a clean history on disk
Creating a verified backup or image of the system and data before upgrading
explain: Even a normally reliable upgrade can fail, so a restorable image or verified backup is the rollback plan if the new installation does not complete.

q: Which Microsoft tool creates bootable Windows installation USB media and downloads the latest image?
options: Windows Easy Transfer, which moves user settings between two Windows PCs
Disk Cleanup, which removes temporary files from a Windows installation
Media Creation Tool, which builds current Windows installation media
File History, which backs up user libraries on a recurring schedule
explain: Microsoft's Media Creation Tool downloads the current Windows image, builds bootable installation media, and can also start an in-place upgrade.

q: On a UEFI system, how must the boot partition on Windows installation media be formatted?
options: As NTFS only, because UEFI firmware reads the boot files from NTFS volumes
As FAT32, because the EFI System Partition must use a format UEFI can read
As exFAT, because the EFI System Partition must use a format UEFI can read
As ext4, because the EFI System Partition must use a format UEFI can read
explain: UEFI firmware reads FAT32 EFI System Partitions, so installers place boot files there even when the Windows operating system volume itself is NTFS.

q: Which requirements are part of the official minimum hardware requirements for Windows 11?
options: TPM 2.0, Secure Boot-capable UEFI firmware, and a supported processor
A touchscreen display, Secure Boot-capable firmware, and a supported processor
32 GB of RAM, Secure Boot-capable firmware, and a supported processor
A discrete graphics card, Secure Boot-capable firmware, and a supported processor
explain: TPM 2.0 and Secure Boot capability are headline Windows 11 requirements, along with a supported CPU. The PC Health Check app validates a specific machine.

q: What is the purpose of Sysprep in Windows image deployment?
options: To activate Windows on the reference computer before the image is captured
To compress the captured image by half before it is deployed to new PCs
To install Microsoft Office on the reference computer before imaging begins
To generalize an installation by removing unique settings so it can be deployed widely
explain: Sysprep with the generalize option removes machine-specific identity such as unique SIDs, preparing a reference installation for capture and deployment to many machines.

q: What does an unattend answer file, such as autounattend.xml, allow an installer to do?
options: Bypass the product key check by generating a valid key during Windows Setup
Bypass hardware requirements checks as a supported part of Windows Setup
Automate Windows Setup choices such as locale, partitions, and product keys
Replace the computer firmware as an automated part of Windows Setup entirely
explain: Answer files supply Setup with its answers during passes such as specialize and oobeSystem, which is a standard part of hands-free enterprise deployment.

q: What does Windows Deployment Services provide for Windows installations?
options: Management of wireless access points across an enterprise network
Network-based deployment of Windows images through PXE boot
Hosting of web applications across an enterprise network
Encryption of disks across an enterprise network of Windows PCs
explain: Windows Deployment Services lets client PCs boot from the network using PXE and pull down captured Windows images for installation.

q: How does a feature update differ from a quality update in Windows Update?
options: Feature updates deliver a new Windows build; quality updates are monthly fixes
Feature updates change the Windows edition; quality updates deliver a new build
Feature updates only fix printer issues; quality updates are monthly fixes
Feature updates and quality updates deliver exactly the same type of changes
explain: Feature updates move the PC to a new Windows version or build on a roughly annual cadence. Quality updates are monthly cumulative security and reliability fixes.

q: After a feature update, how long does Windows keep the previous installation available for rollback by default?
options: For 24 hours after the update, before the previous installation is removed
For 90 days after the update, before the previous installation is removed
Indefinitely after the update, because the previous installation is never removed
For about 10 days after the update, before Windows.old is removed automatically
explain: The rollback window defaults to about 10 days. Disk Cleanup or Storage Sense can remove the previous installation in Windows.old sooner than that.

q: How can an administrator uninstall a problematic quality update from Windows?
options: Through Device Manager, by rolling back the driver for the update package
Through the Microsoft Store, by removing the update from the app library
Through Update history and Uninstall updates, or by using wusa with the uninstall switch
Through Task Scheduler, by deleting the task that installed the update package
explain: Update history provides an uninstall path for most quality updates, and wusa can remove a package by its KB number. WinRE and DISM can remove packages offline.

q: Windows Update repeatedly fails with corruption errors despite restarts. Which repair sequence is the appropriate deeper step?
options: Formatting the drive and reinstalling Windows as the immediate next repair step
Stopping the update services, renaming SoftwareDistribution and catroot2, then restarting the services
Disabling Windows Update permanently so the corruption errors stop being reported
Deleting the registry hives so Windows rebuilds the update configuration from scratch
explain: Resetting the update download cache and components is the standard escalation for repeated corruption errors, followed by DISM and System File Checker if needed.

q: Which methods can be used to reach the Windows Recovery Environment?
options: Holding Shift while choosing Restart, using Recovery settings, or after repeated boot failures
Pressing F12 during startup, but only on computers made by one specific manufacturer
Unplugging the PC three times, which is the only supported way to enter the environment
Starting in Safe Mode, which is the only supported way to enter the environment from Windows
explain: Shift plus Restart and the Advanced startup option in Recovery settings both boot into WinRE, and Windows also enters it automatically after repeated boot failures.

q: What are Windows virtual desktops, accessed through Task View, used to do?
options: Run multiple full copies of Windows at the same time on one computer
Increase the resolution of the connected monitor beyond its native setting
Organize open apps into separate workspaces that can be switched between quickly
Back up desktop icons and window positions to a recovery file automatically
explain: Virtual desktops are a window-management feature for grouping apps into workspaces. They are not virtual machines, and apps keep running across desktops.

q: How does System Restore in WinRE differ from System Image Recovery?
options: It restores an entire disk image captured at an earlier point in time
It deletes personal documents while restoring the operating system files
It rolls back system files, registry, and drivers to a restore point without touching personal files
It requires a second computer to supply the files needed for the restore
explain: Restore points are lightweight snapshots of system state, so System Restore can undo system changes without affecting personal files. Image recovery restores a whole volume.

q: A PC blue-screens after a driver update. What is the fastest recovery using Startup Settings in WinRE?
options: Formatting the operating system drive and reinstalling Windows from media
Booting into Safe Mode and rolling back or uninstalling the new driver
Running Windows Memory Diagnostics continuously for a full day of testing
Resetting the firmware password and then reinstalling Windows from media
explain: Safe Mode loads a minimal driver set, so the PC can usually start well enough for the offending driver to be rolled back or uninstalled.

q: When is disabling driver signature enforcement from Startup Settings appropriately used?
options: When installing a legitimate legacy or test driver that is not signed, for that boot only
When Windows will not activate and the product key needs to be entered again manually
When the system disk is full and additional space needs to be created immediately
When a user has forgotten the sign-in password and needs to reset it from startup
explain: The setting lasts for one boot and exists for legitimate legacy hardware. Permanently disabling signature checks would be a lasting security risk.

q: How can a technician open a command prompt for offline repairs on a PC that will not boot?
options: Through the Ease of Access button on the sign-in screen, as the standard repair path
Through BIOS setup, by selecting the command prompt page in the firmware menus
Through Safe Mode with Networking only, as the standard offline repair path to use
Through WinRE, under Troubleshoot, Advanced options, and then Command Prompt
explain: The WinRE command prompt runs offline against the installed Windows copy, so boot and system files can be repaired even when Windows itself will not start.

q: In the WinRE command prompt, why does the installed Windows volume often appear under a different drive letter?
options: Because the drive is encrypted, WinRE assigns it a temporary letter for repairs
Because the command prompt is malfunctioning, WinRE assigns letters inconsistently
Because WinRE assigns letters in its own order, so the volume must be verified first
Because drive letters are assigned randomly each time WinRE starts a repair session
explain: WinRE builds its own drive-letter assignments, so a technician should confirm the real Windows volume, for example with diskpart list volume, before running repairs.

q: Which command form runs System File Checker against an offline Windows installation?
options: sfc /offline, with no additional path information for the target installation
sfc /scannow with the offbootdir and offwindir switches pointing to the target
Plain sfc /scannow in WinRE, which automatically targets the offline installation
DISM in online mode, which automatically targets the offline installation instead
explain: Offline System File Checker needs the boot directory and Windows directory of the target installation, because it is not running inside that copy of Windows.

q: Which command form lets DISM service an offline Windows image?
options: DISM with the Image switch pointing to the offline Windows directory
chkdsk with an image switch pointing to the offline Windows directory
defrag with an offline switch pointing to the offline Windows directory
format with an image switch pointing to the offline Windows directory
explain: The /Image switch points DISM at a mounted or offline Windows directory instead of the running operating system, and a source can be supplied if needed.

q: What can a USB recovery drive created from a working Windows PC do?
options: Recover a forgotten Microsoft account password for the PC's signed-in user
Repair hardware failures that prevent the PC from completing its startup tests
Back up user documents automatically whenever the drive is connected to the PC
Boot a non-booting PC into WinRE and, if system files were included, reinstall Windows
explain: A recovery USB is bootable repair media. Including system files when it is created adds the option of a bare-metal reinstall of Windows.

q: When is Reset this PC with Remove everything and Cloud download the best choice?
options: When the user wants to keep all installed apps exactly as they are now
When there is no internet connection and no installation media available
When the local recovery image may be corrupt and a clean Windows is desired
When only the desktop wallpaper and theme settings are not working correctly
explain: Cloud download fetches a pristine Windows image from Microsoft, bypassing local recovery files that may themselves be damaged.

q: What will a BitLocker-protected drive prompt for when repairs are attempted in WinRE?
options: Only the user's PIN, in every case where WinRE needs to access the drive
The 48-digit recovery key, before the volume can be unlocked for repairs
Nothing, because WinRE is able to bypass BitLocker encryption for repairs
A new Windows license, before the volume can be unlocked for any repairs
explain: WinRE cannot read an encrypted volume until it is unlocked, so the BitLocker recovery key is required before repair tools can access the drive.

q: A PC fails after a RAM upgrade, beeping and looping before POST completes. Why are Windows recovery tools not relevant to this failure?
options: The failure is at the hardware and POST level, before any OS or recovery environment loads
The recovery environment requires a password that the user has not yet provided to anyone
The recovery partition is hidden, so the recovery tools cannot be started from the keyboard
Safe Mode has been disabled, so the recovery tools cannot be started from the startup menu
explain: A no-POST fault is a hardware or firmware problem. Operating system recovery can only begin after firmware successfully hands off to a boot loader.

q: Windows Setup reports that Windows cannot be installed to an MBR disk on a UEFI system. What is the installer-side fix?
options: Formatting the installation USB as NTFS so Setup can use the MBR disk as it is
Disabling Secure Boot permanently so Setup can use the MBR disk as it is now
Installing Windows to the recovery partition so the MBR disk layout can stay as is
Deleting the partitions so Setup can create a GPT layout, accepting that data will be lost
explain: UEFI mode requires a GPT disk for installation. Setup can reinitialize an emptied disk as GPT during a custom install, or the disk can be converted beforehand.

q: What does Microsoft's MBR2GPT tool do for a Windows disk?
options: It converts a volume from the FAT32 file system to the NTFS file system
It repairs the Boot Configuration Data store on an MBR disk in place
It converts a Windows disk from MBR to GPT in place without data loss
It creates bootable Windows installation media from an ISO image file
explain: When validation passes, mbr2gpt can validate and then convert a system disk in place, migrating a BIOS-based installation to UEFI and GPT without wiping it.

q: What does an in-place upgrade from Windows 10 to Windows 11 keep on a PC?
options: Nothing, because the upgrade is always performed as a clean installation
Files, settings, and compatible applications, when done as an in-place upgrade
Only files that are stored in the Recycle Bin at the time of the upgrade
Only the desktop wallpaper and theme settings at the time of the upgrade
explain: An in-place upgrade through Setup or Windows Update preserves the user environment, including files, settings, and compatible applications.

q: Windows Update reports that a PC does not currently meet the requirements for Windows 11. What should the technician do first?
options: Run PC Health Check to identify the specific blocker and address it in firmware if supported
Install Windows 11 anyway using registry changes as the first response to the message
Tell the user to buy a new PC immediately as the first response to the message received
Disable Windows Update so the requirements message stops appearing on the PC entirely
explain: Most blockers are firmware settings, such as a disabled TPM or Secure Boot, rather than truly missing hardware, so the specific blocker should be identified first.

q: What does the Windows.old folder contain after an upgrade?
options: Old printer drivers that were replaced during the upgrade process only
User accounts that were deleted during the upgrade process only entirely
A backup copy of the paging file created during the upgrade process
The previous Windows installation, kept for rollback and manual file recovery
explain: Windows.old holds the previous operating system tree for about 10 days, serving both as the rollback source and as a place to rescue files after a bad upgrade.

q: How does Safe Mode with Networking differ from plain Safe Mode in Windows?
options: It enables the full graphics drivers that plain Safe Mode leaves disabled entirely
It disables the Windows firewall that plain Safe Mode leaves enabled entirely
It also loads network drivers and services so tools and shares can be reached
It allows full domain Group Policy processing that plain Safe Mode skips entirely
explain: The Networking variant adds network adapter drivers and related services to the minimal Safe Mode environment, which helps with downloads but adds some risk during malware cleanup.

q: What does Safe Mode with Command Prompt boot into on a Windows PC?
options: A Linux shell that is included as a fallback in the Windows installation
A minimal environment that opens a command window instead of the Explorer shell
The firmware setup utility that is included in the computer's BIOS menus
A text-mode installer that is included as a fallback in the Windows installation
explain: This Startup Settings option replaces the Explorer shell with a command window, which is a useful fallback when Explorer itself crashes at sign-in.

q: When does the Enable low-resolution video option in Startup Settings help a technician?
options: When a bad display setting or driver leaves the screen unreadable at native settings
When the graphics processor has physically failed and cannot produce any output at all
When the monitor has been unplugged from the computer and cannot be detected at all
When Windows has not been activated and the display settings are locked by licensing
explain: Low-resolution video loads a basic display path, so a technician can get a readable screen and then restore the correct driver or display settings.

q: A PC repeatedly shows Preparing automatic repair and then fails to start. What does that loop most often indicate?
options: A healthy system that simply needs several more restart attempts to finish starting
A slow internet connection that is delaying the download of the startup repair files
A dirty keyboard that is sending incorrect input during the startup repair process
Corrupt boot or startup components, or a failing disk, to investigate from WinRE
explain: Automatic Repair loops usually point to Boot Configuration Data or startup corruption, or to failing disk hardware, and should be diagnosed from WinRE.

q: Why will a PC that is upgraded to a new motherboard usually need Windows to be reactivated?
options: Because the hard drive's assigned letters changed during the motherboard upgrade process
Because additional RAM was installed at the same time as the motherboard upgrade itself
Because the digital license is tied to the previous hardware ID, which was the motherboard
Because a new monitor was connected at the same time as the motherboard upgrade itself
explain: A motherboard change creates a significantly different hardware hash. Linking the license to a Microsoft account allows the Activation troubleshooter to transfer it.

q: What happens during the OOBE phase of Windows Setup?
options: Drivers for the computer's hardware are compiled from source during this phase
The user creates the first account and chooses privacy and region settings
The system disk is partitioned and formatted in preparation for installation
Windows updates are downloaded and installed before the first account is created
explain: OOBE, the Out-Of-Box Experience, is the first-run phase after installation, where the first account and regional and privacy choices are made.

q: Choosing an offline setup option during OOBE historically allowed a user to create what instead?
options: A local account instead of a Microsoft account, where that option was offered
An administrator account that requires no password to sign in to Windows
A domain account without contacting a domain controller on the network
A second Windows installation alongside the one that Setup just created
explain: Home editions encourage a Microsoft account, but offline paths, where offered, created a local account instead. Enterprises use deployment tools for this.

q: Installing Windows from an ISO mounted in File Explorer is suitable for which task?
options: A bare-metal installation on an empty disk with no other media available at all
A firmware update that must be applied before Windows Setup can run on the PC
Formatting the running system drive from inside the Windows session using the ISO
An in-place upgrade or repair launched from within a running Windows installation
explain: Mounting an ISO and running setup.exe from inside Windows is the classic path for an in-place upgrade or repair install, not for an empty-disk installation.

q: Before an image is deployed to 500 identical laptops, how should the reference machine be prepared?
options: It should be activated with a retail key and left running for the capture process
It should be joined to the domain and used as a normal workstation before capture
It should be generalized with Sysprep, shut down, and then captured as the image
It should be filled with the technician's working files before the capture process
explain: Generalizing removes unique identifiers so each deployed laptop generates fresh SIDs and runs its own setup passes on first boot.

q: How is Windows activation typically handled after imaging PCs with a volume license?
options: By calling Microsoft manually for each machine as it is deployed to a user
By KMS or Active Directory-Based Activation automatically on the network or domain
By entering the same retail key manually on each machine as it is deployed
By skipping activation permanently on each machine as it is deployed to a user
explain: Volume images carry a generic KMS client key, so activation happens automatically against the organization's KMS host or through Active Directory-Based Activation.

q: When is an in-place upgrade repair, also called a repair install, the appropriate choice?
options: To fix deep Windows corruption while keeping files, settings, and installed apps
To recover photos that were permanently deleted from the user's Documents folder
To upgrade the Windows edition to Enterprise without buying a new license key
To remove the need to keep backups of the system and data on the computer
explain: Running Setup over the existing installation refreshes the system files while preserving the environment, making it the last step before a clean install.

q: Using only built-in Windows tools on a UEFI machine, how can a technician create a bootable installer from an ISO?
options: By renaming the ISO file to an executable and copying it to a USB drive as is
By copying the ISO file alone onto an NTFS USB drive in every case without changes
By using the Snipping Tool to capture the ISO contents onto a USB drive for booting
By formatting a USB drive as FAT32 and copying the ISO contents, splitting install.wim if needed
explain: UEFI can boot from a FAT32 USB drive containing the extracted Setup files. A large install.wim must be split because FAT32 cannot store a file over 4 GB.

q: Through which settings can the default operating system and boot menu timeout be chosen on a dual-boot PC?
options: Disk Cleanup, through the system files cleanup options for the boot volume
The Microsoft Store, through the library settings for the installed Windows apps
System Properties Startup and Recovery, the msconfig Boot tab, or bcdedit
Device Manager, through the properties of the disk drive holding the boot volume
explain: Boot menu behavior is stored in the Boot Configuration Data, and it can be edited through Startup and Recovery settings, msconfig, or bcdedit.

q: The boot menu shows two entries both named Windows 11 after an upgrade. What does the extra entry usually point to?
options: A virus infection, in every case where duplicate boot entries appear after an upgrade
A leftover or second installation that can be removed after verifying which volume it boots
The recovery partition, which presents itself as a full Windows installation at boot time
A Linux installation, which presents itself under the Windows name in the boot menu
explain: Stale Boot Configuration Data entries are common after in-place upgrade work. Each entry's target volume should be verified before an entry is deleted.

q: Why should recovery partitions generally not be deleted casually from a Windows PC?
options: They hold the WinRE tools needed for resets and repairs, so removing them breaks recovery
They contain the user's personal documents, so removing them deletes the user's main files
They make the PC run faster while present, so removing them noticeably slows the computer
They are required for internet access, so removing them disconnects the computer entirely
explain: The recovery partition holds the Windows Recovery Environment used for resets and repairs. It can be rebuilt after deletion, but only with additional effort.

q: macOS Finder is the equivalent of which Windows component?
options: Task Manager, which manages running processes and startup programs on Windows
File Explorer, which provides file management and the desktop shell on Windows
Control Panel, which provides system settings and configuration pages on Windows
Disk Management, which provides volume and partition management on Windows
explain: Finder is the Mac's file manager and desktop shell, performing the same role that File Explorer performs on Windows.

q: What does Mission Control provide on a Mac?
options: An overview of all open windows, desktops in Spaces, and full-screen apps
A dashboard for scheduling and reviewing Time Machine backup jobs
A console for scanning the Mac for malware and removing threats found
A console for managing printers and print queues shared from the Mac
explain: Mission Control exposes every open window, Space, and full-screen app in one overview, and it can be opened with F3 or a three-finger swipe up.

q: What is Spotlight used to do on a Mac?
options: Clean temporary files and caches from the Mac's internal storage drive
Manage user accounts and sign-in settings for people who use the Mac
Update the Mac's firmware to the latest version provided by Apple
Search files, apps, and information across the Mac from one place
explain: Spotlight is the system-wide search on macOS, opened with Command plus Space, and it also provides quick calculations and definitions.

q: What does Gatekeeper enforce on a Mac?
options: Firewall rules that control which network connections apps can make
Disk encryption settings that control how volumes on the Mac are protected
Which sources apps may be installed from, with checks when apps first launch
Screen time limits that control how long apps on the Mac can be used daily
explain: Gatekeeper verifies code signing and notarization when an app is first opened and limits installation sources to the App Store or identified developers.

q: What does Rosetta 2 allow on a Mac with Apple silicon?
options: Windows to boot natively as the primary operating system on the Mac
Apps built for Intel Macs to run through code translation on the Mac
iOS apps to be sideloaded as the only way to run them on the Mac at all
32-bit kernel extensions to load as system extensions on the Mac at all
explain: Rosetta 2 translates Intel x86-64 code to ARM, at install time or first launch, so existing Intel apps can run on Apple silicon with a minor performance cost.

q: What did Boot Camp historically allow on Intel-based Macs?
options: Dual-booting Windows natively on a separate partition of the Mac drive
Running two different versions of macOS side by side on the Mac drive
Virtualizing iOS as a guest operating system on the Mac drive for testing
Booting Linux only, as the sole guest operating system on the Mac drive
explain: Boot Camp Assistant partitioned the drive and supported a native Windows installation on Intel Macs. It is not available on Apple silicon Macs.

q: How is macOS Recovery entered on a Mac with Apple silicon?
options: By holding Command plus R only, while the Mac is starting up from being off
By pressing F8 repeatedly, while the Mac is starting up from being off entirely
By booting from a DVD, while the Mac is starting up from being off entirely
By holding the power button at startup until startup options appear, then choosing Options
explain: Apple silicon Macs use the startup options screen reached by holding the power button. Intel Macs instead use Command plus R and its variants.

q: What does the First Aid feature in macOS Disk Utility do for a volume?
options: Defragments the volume to consolidate free space
Erases saved passwords stored on the volume
Checks the volume for filesystem errors and repairs them
Downloads and installs pending macOS updates
explain: First Aid verifies and repairs filesystem directory structures on a Mac volume, serving a role similar to chkdsk on Windows.

q: What does Keychain Access on macOS store for a user?
options: Printer settings and saved print queues
Passwords, certificates, and secure notes
Boot options and startup disk settings
System logs and diagnostic reports
explain: Keychain Access stores passwords, certificates, and secure notes; the login keychain unlocks with the user's account password.

q: What is FileVault on macOS?
options: Full-disk encryption for the startup disk
A file-sharing service for local networks
A password manager for web browsers only
A cloud storage service for documents
explain: FileVault 2 encrypts the entire startup volume and is unlocked at pre-boot by authorized users or a recovery key.

q: A Mac app has stopped responding. How should you force it to quit?
options: Press Control+Alt+Delete and select the app
Hold the power button until the Mac shuts down
Empty the Trash to release the app's memory
Press Command+Option+Esc and use the Force Quit window
explain: Command+Option+Esc opens the Force Quit window, the Mac equivalent of ending a hung task in Task Manager.

q: A Mac starts up to a flashing question-mark folder icon. What does this indicate?
options: The battery has completely discharged
The display has failed and cannot show the desktop
No bootable system was found on a startup volume
Wi-Fi is turned off so macOS cannot load
explain: The flashing question mark means the firmware could not find a valid startup volume, pointing to a disk or operating system problem.

q: Which macOS utility is the equivalent of Windows Task Manager for viewing and ending processes?
options: Console, which displays system log messages
Activity Monitor, which lists processes and resource use
Disk Utility, which manages volumes and disks
System Information, which lists hardware details
explain: Activity Monitor shows processes and resource use and can force-quit them, while Console is used to read logs.

q: What does the Linux sudo command do?
options: Runs a single command with elevated root privileges after the user authenticates
Switches the entire shell permanently to another user account
Schedules a command to run at a specified future time
Encrypts the user's home folder with a passphrase
explain: sudo grants temporary root privileges for a single command after authentication, whereas su switches the whole shell to another user.

q: What does a Linux package manager such as apt or dnf do?
options: Downloads installation ISO images for new systems
Manages user passwords and account policies
Partitions and formats disks during installation
Installs, updates, and removes software packages and their dependencies
explain: Package managers install, update, and remove software from repositories while resolving and tracking dependencies.

q: How does apt update differ from apt upgrade in Linux?
options: Update deletes old packages, while upgrade keeps them
Update upgrades the kernel only, while upgrade updates applications
Update only refreshes the package lists, while upgrade installs the newer versions
Update requires a reboot, while upgrade never does
explain: apt update only refreshes the package lists; apt upgrade is the step that actually installs newer package versions.

q: In a Linux shell, what does the ~ symbol refer to?
options: The root directory of the filesystem
The current user's home directory
The system temporary folder
The directory visited immediately before this one
explain: The tilde expands to the current user's home directory ($HOME); / is the root directory and .. is the parent directory.

q: What does the /etc directory in Linux primarily contain?
options: System-wide configuration files
Documents created by regular users
Log files generated by running services
Temporary files created by applications
explain: /etc holds system-wide configuration files; logs are mainly under /var and temporary files under /tmp.

q: What is the grep command in Linux used for?
options: Compressing files into a single archive
Copying directories and their contents
Listing the hardware installed in the system
Searching text in files or piped output for matching patterns
explain: grep filters lines that match a pattern, which makes it central to searching logs and other text output.

q: What does the Linux man command provide?
options: A list of users currently signed in
Network statistics for active connections
Manual pages that document commands and their options
A list of updates available for installation
explain: Running man followed by a command name opens the installed reference documentation for that command.

q: What is the tar command in Linux primarily used for?
options: Editing text files in the terminal
Creating and extracting archive files, often compressed as .tar.gz
Monitoring running processes and resource use
Formatting disks and creating filesystems
explain: tar bundles files into archives; compression is commonly added with gzip, producing .tar.gz files.

q: A Linux file has permissions rwxr-xr--. What access does this give?
options: The owner can read, write, and execute; the group can read and execute; others can only read
The owner can only read; the group can execute; others have no access at all
The owner can execute only; the group can write; others can read and write
The owner has no access; the group can read; others can read, write, and execute
explain: Read the triplets left to right: owner rwx, group r-x, and others r--.

q: How are ChromeOS devices managed at scale in an organization?
options: Through Windows Group Policy applied to each device
Through Apple School Manager device assignments
Through local accounts configured on each device
Through the Google Admin console and Chrome management policies
explain: The Google Admin console applies Chrome management policies fleet-wide, controlling apps, extensions, updates, and restrictions.

q: How are ChromeOS updates delivered and applied?
options: Only from USB installation media created by IT
Through the Microsoft Store update service
Automatically in the background to an idle A/B partition, then applied at reboot
Manually, by each user downloading an installer file
explain: ChromeOS keeps two system partitions, installs updates to the idle one in the background, and swaps to it at restart, allowing rollback if needed.

q: How does the Linux environment on Chromebooks (Crostini) run Linux apps?
options: By dual-booting the device into a Linux installation
Inside a container within a virtual machine, isolated from ChromeOS
With full direct access to the host kernel settings
Only after the device is placed in developer mode
explain: Crostini runs Linux apps in a container inside a virtual machine, keeping them sandboxed from the verified ChromeOS system.

q: On a managed Chromebook, when can an admin policy block a user from starting a powerwash from Settings?
options: When an admin policy disables factory reset for enrolled devices
When the battery charge falls below 100 percent
When the device is not connected to Wi-Fi
When the device is being used in tablet mode
explain: Enterprise enrollment can disable factory reset (powerwash) by policy, keeping managed Chromebooks under admin control.

q: How does verified boot protect ChromeOS at startup?
options: It encrypts user files a second time at boot
It requires a password to be entered at every boot
It blocks all Linux apps from starting
It checks firmware and OS integrity and restores the known-good copy if tampering is found
explain: Verified boot checks the integrity of the firmware and OS at startup and, with the A/B partition design, can restore a known-good image.

q: What does Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL) allow a Windows user to do?
options: Boot Linux instead of Windows as the only system
Run macOS applications directly on Windows
Run a genuine Linux environment and command-line tools directly on Windows
Replace PowerShell with a Linux desktop environment
explain: WSL lets users run a real Linux environment and command-line tools on Windows; WSL 2 uses a lightweight virtual machine with a real Linux kernel.

q: Where can you view and enable installed optional Windows features such as Telnet Client or .NET 3.5?
options: In Device Manager under optional devices
In 'Turn Windows features on or off' (OptionalFeatures)
In Disk Cleanup under system files
In the BIOS setup under advanced features
explain: The Windows Features dialog toggles optional components such as .NET Framework 3.5, Hyper-V, Telnet Client, and WSL.

q: Why does .NET Framework 3.5 installation fail online on some PCs, and how is it installed instead?
options: It must be sourced from Windows Update or installation media as a feature on demand
It must always be purchased separately from Microsoft
It must be installed from the printer driver package
It must first be enabled in the BIOS setup
explain: .NET Framework 3.5 is a Feature on Demand, so offline systems need Windows Update or installation media as the source, for example with DISM /Source.

q: What is Windows 'God Mode' an informal name for?
options: A hidden built-in administrator account
A registry edit that overclocks Windows
Safe Mode with networking enabled
A folder shortcut that lists all Control Panel tasks in one view
explain: God Mode is a shell folder shortcut that aggregates every Control Panel task in one list; it is a convenience, not a privilege escalation.

q: Why is the Windows Reliability Monitor useful when troubleshooting?
options: It defragments disks on a schedule
It tests system RAM for hardware errors
It shows a timeline of crashes, failures, and updates so problems can be correlated with changes
It manages which apps run at startup
explain: Reliability Monitor presents a timeline of application crashes, Windows failures, and updates, making it easy to see when instability began.

q: What does Windows Memory Diagnostic test?
options: The hard drive's SMART health status
System RAM for errors, running at reboot outside Windows
The GPU for graphics rendering errors
The page file for corruption errors
explain: Windows Memory Diagnostic (mdsched) tests system RAM during a reboot, outside Windows, and reports results in Event Viewer after sign-in.

q: A PC is suspected of having RAM errors but passes a quick test. What should the technician understand?
options: Intermittent errors may need extended or multiple test passes to surface
One 30-second pass is definitive proof the RAM is good
RAM cannot fail after it has been purchased and installed
RAM errors only occur when Windows runs in Safe Mode
explain: Marginal RAM can pass a short test; extended or repeated passes are often needed to expose heat- or timing-related faults.

q: What do SideBySide errors and sxstrace results in Event Viewer usually relate to?
options: Disk fragmentation on the system volume
Network adapter driver failures
Printer spooler service failures
Visual C++ runtime or assembly conflicts for older applications
explain: SideBySide errors mean an application requested a Visual C++ runtime version that is missing or corrupt; installing the correct redistributable usually fixes it.

q: What can Compatibility Mode do for a legacy Windows application?
options: Emulate a faster CPU for the application
Provide additional RAM to the application
Emulate earlier Windows behavior and apply settings such as reduced color mode and DPI scaling overrides
Convert the application to a different file system
explain: Compatibility Mode and the Program Compatibility Troubleshooter apply shims that emulate earlier Windows versions and settings for old applications.

q: How are high-DPI scaling problems, such as blurry legacy apps, usually addressed in Windows?
options: By permanently lowering the monitor's native resolution
Through the app's Compatibility settings by overriding DPI scaling behavior
By disabling ClearType for all applications
By reinstalling Windows with a lower display driver
explain: Per-app DPI scaling overrides in Compatibility settings (System or Application) fix blurry or incorrectly sized legacy windows on high-resolution displays.

q: Which built-in Windows feature provides screen recording for apps when you press Win+G?
options: The Xbox Game Bar overlay
The Snipping Tool capture bar only
The Paint accessories application
The Windows Fax and Scan utility
explain: The Xbox Game Bar (Win+G) records app windows and captures clips and screenshots, which is also useful for documenting reproduction steps.

q: Sticky Keys, Filter Keys, and Toggle Keys are examples of what type of Windows feature?
options: Gaming macros for keyboard shortcuts
BIOS options for keyboard behavior
Printer settings for accessibility forms
Accessibility (Ease of Access) keyboard features
explain: These are Ease of Access keyboard features that assist users with motor impairments; pressing Shift five times can accidentally trigger Sticky Keys.

q: What needs do Narrator and Magnifier serve in Windows?
options: Dictation of documents into applications only
Color calibration of the display for printing
Screen reading with text-to-speech and screen magnification for users with low vision
Faster scrolling through long documents
explain: Narrator reads the interface aloud and Magnifier enlarges portions of the screen, both supporting users with low vision.

q: What are the three classic authentication factor categories?
options: Something you know, something you type, and something you see
Passwords, PINs, and unlock patterns
Something you know, something you have, and something you are
Hardware, software, and firmware
explain: The factor families are knowledge (something you know), possession (something you have), and inherence (something you are); a password plus a PIN is still only one factor family.

q: How does a time-based one-time password (TOTP) authenticator app generate codes?
options: It receives codes by text message from the service
It generates codes from a shared secret and the current time, rotating about every 30 seconds
It retrieves the account password stored by the service
It generates codes from the phone's current location
explain: TOTP derives codes from a shared seed plus the current time step, which is why an inaccurate device clock can cause valid codes to be rejected.

q: Why do passkeys (FIDO2/WebAuthn) improve on passwords?
options: They are phishing-resistant because the credential is bound to the legitimate site's origin
They are shorter and faster for users to type
They are stored in a plain text file for recovery
They can be reused across all sites and services
explain: With passkeys, the private key never leaves the authenticator and the authentication challenge is bound to the site's origin, defeating look-alike phishing sites.

q: In Kerberos, why is a user issued a Ticket Granting Ticket (TGT) after initial logon?
options: To encrypt the user's hard drive at startup
To bypass multifactor authentication prompts
To reset other users' passwords when needed
To request service tickets for resources without re-entering credentials
explain: The TGT proves the user authenticated to the Key Distribution Center, which then issues per-service tickets, enabling single sign-on in Active Directory.

q: What are SAML and OpenID Connect primarily used for?
options: Encrypting disks on user endpoints
Managing Wi-Fi passwords for clients
Federated single sign-on between identity providers and applications
Patching browsers across the organization
explain: SAML and OpenID Connect provide federated single sign-on, letting one identity provider authenticate users to many applications.

q: How does TACACS+ differ from RADIUS?
options: TACACS+ is used only for wireless authentication
TACACS+ uses TCP and encrypts the entire payload, while RADIUS uses UDP and encrypts only the password
TACACS+ cannot perform accounting of user actions
TACACS+ is a protocol developed only by Microsoft
explain: TACACS+ separates AAA functions, uses TCP, and encrypts the entire payload; RADIUS uses UDP and encrypts only the password field.

q: Port security on a switch with 'sticky' MAC learning does what?
options: Learns and saves the MAC addresses allowed on a port and can shut the port down on a violation
Encrypts all traffic on the port
Assigns IP addresses
Blocks all broadcast traffic
explain: Sticky port security binds a port to known devices to prevent unauthorized swaps and rogue connections.

q: How does DHCP snooping protect a LAN?
options: It encrypts all DHCP traffic between clients
It assigns static IP addresses to all clients
It disables DHCP relay agents on the network
It blocks rogue DHCP servers from answering on untrusted ports
explain: DHCP snooping builds a binding table of legitimate leases and drops DHCP server responses arriving on untrusted ports.

q: How does Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI) prevent ARP spoofing?
options: It encrypts all ARP traffic on the network
It disables ARP entirely on protected VLANs
It validates ARP packets against the DHCP snooping binding table
It assigns static IP addresses to servers only
explain: DAI checks ARP messages against known IP-to-MAC bindings from DHCP snooping, blocking ARP poisoning used for man-in-the-middle attacks.

q: What are the three roles in an 802.1X deployment?
options: Client, proxy, and gateway
Supplicant (client), authenticator (switch or AP), and authentication server (RADIUS)
User, administrator, and auditor
Access point, controller, and cloud service
explain: In 802.1X, the authenticator passes EAP messages between the supplicant and the RADIUS authentication server until access is granted or denied.

q: Why is EAP-TLS considered the strongest common EAP method?
options: Both the client and the server authenticate with certificates, providing mutual authentication
It needs no certificates on clients or servers
It derives its keys from legacy WEP keys
It is the fastest EAP method to deploy
explain: EAP-TLS provides mutual certificate authentication for client and server, removing password-based weaknesses at the cost of more complex deployment.

q: What might Network Access Control (NAC) posture assessment check on a connecting device?
options: The job title of the user signing in
The resale value of the connecting device
Printer compatibility for the device
Current patches, antivirus status, disk encryption, and an enabled firewall before granting access
explain: NAC enforces endpoint health policies before granting access and can quarantine non-compliant devices to a remediation VLAN.

q: Why do credential stuffing attacks succeed?
options: Target sites use weak encryption for passwords
Firewall rules are missing on the target site
Users reuse the same password across many sites, so breached credentials unlock other accounts
Password hashing on the target site is too slow
explain: Attackers replay breached username and password pairs at scale; unique passwords for each site and MFA defeat credential stuffing.

q: What does the principle of least privilege mean?
options: Administrators share one account for convenience
Users and processes get only the minimum access required for their tasks
Everyone gets read access to all resources
Passwords are set to never expire for users
explain: Least privilege gives users and processes only the access their tasks require, limiting the damage from mistakes or compromised accounts.

q: How does just-in-time (JIT) privileged access improve security?
options: It grants admin rights only when needed and for a limited time instead of standing privileges
It gives administrators permanent rights more quickly
It removes approval workflows for privileged access
It shares the domain admin password with technicians
explain: JIT elevation through privileged access management tools shrinks the window in which powerful rights exist and could be abused.

q: How does Windows LAPS protect against lateral movement?
options: It disables the local admin account's password entirely
It sets the same local admin password on all PCs
It removes local admin accounts from the OS
It randomizes and centrally manages a unique local admin password on every machine
explain: LAPS gives each machine a unique, centrally managed local admin password, so one cracked password cannot be reused across the fleet.

q: How does Credential Guard on Windows protect secrets?
options: It stores passwords in a protected text file
It disables NTLM authentication on printers
It isolates LSASS credential material inside a virtualization-based secure enclave
It encrypts the page file and nothing else
explain: Credential Guard uses virtualization-based security to isolate credential material in LSASS from the normal OS memory that theft tools scrape.

q: How does Controlled Folder Access in Windows Security help stop ransomware?
options: It backs up user files to removable DVDs
It blocks untrusted apps from writing to protected folders such as Documents
It encrypts the entire Windows registry
It disables the keyboard when encryption is detected
explain: Controlled Folder Access prevents untrusted processes from modifying protected folders, blunting mass file encryption by ransomware.

q: What does memory integrity (HVCI / core isolation) enforce in Windows?
options: Kernel code integrity using virtualization-based security, blocking unsigned kernel code
Faster boot times through kernel caching
Automatic updates for all device drivers
Encryption of all Wi-Fi network traffic
explain: Memory integrity (HVCI) uses virtualization-based security to ensure only trusted code runs in kernel mode, defending against malicious drivers.

q: Why is BitLocker with TPM+PIN stronger than TPM-only BitLocker?
options: It makes the encryption process run faster
It removes the need for a recovery key
It works on machines without a TPM chip
It adds a knowledge factor at pre-boot, so a stolen powered-off machine cannot auto-unlock just by having the TPM
explain: TPM-only protection transparently unseals the key for anyone who boots the machine; a pre-boot PIN adds a knowledge factor that stops offline attacks on stolen hardware.

q: What does BitLocker To Go apply to?
options: Network shares hosted on file servers
Cloud storage accounts synced to the PC
Removable drives such as USB sticks and external drives
Printers shared from the workstation
explain: BitLocker To Go encrypts removable media such as USB sticks and external drives, prompting for a password when used on other machines.

q: Why are salted, slow hashing algorithms such as bcrypt used to store passwords?
options: They encrypt passwords so they can be reversed later
Salts defeat rainbow tables and the deliberate slowness makes brute force expensive
They make stored passwords shorter to save space
They synchronize passwords across multiple sites
explain: Passwords are stored as one-way hashes; a unique salt per password defeats rainbow tables and bcrypt's slowness raises the cost of brute-force attacks.

q: In PKI, what is a Certificate Signing Request (CSR)?
options: A request containing a public key and identity information, sent to a CA to be signed into a certificate
A backup copy of a certificate's private key
A notice that a certificate has been revoked
A root certificate issued by a public CA
explain: A CSR contains the public key and identity details; the CA validates the identity and signs it into a certificate while the private key never leaves the requester.

q: What does a wildcard certificate for *.example.com cover?
options: Every domain the company owns
Only the example.com domain itself
Second-level subdomains such as a.b.example.com
All first-level subdomains of example.com, such as mail.example.com
explain: A wildcard certificate matches one label deep, covering first-level subdomains such as mail.example.com, but not deeper names such as a.b.example.com.

q: What is the main risk of using self-signed certificates on internal sites?
options: They expire much more slowly than CA certificates
They use too much CPU on the web server
Users are trained to click through trust warnings, and there is no third-party identity validation
They cannot encrypt traffic between client and server
explain: Self-signed certificates can encrypt traffic but provide no chain of trust, and routinely bypassing their warnings trains users to ignore real certificate errors.

q: How is a certificate's revocation status checked?
options: Only through DNS TXT records for the domain
Through a CRL (revocation list) or OCSP (online status query)
Through a value stored in the Windows registry
By pinging the certificate authority's server
explain: Revocation is checked with CRLs, which are periodically published signed lists, or OCSP, which provides real-time status responses.

q: Why are TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 deprecated?
options: They rely on weak cryptographic algorithms and are vulnerable to known attacks
They are too fast for modern web servers
Browsers never supported either protocol version
They require IPv6 to be enabled to function
explain: TLS 1.0 and 1.1 rely on weak cryptography vulnerable to known attacks, and modern standards such as PCI DSS require TLS 1.2 or higher.

q: Why does TLS use symmetric encryption for bulk data and asymmetric encryption for key exchange?
options: Asymmetric encryption cannot encrypt data at all
Symmetric keys never need to be protected
TLS uses only asymmetric encryption for all data
Symmetric algorithms are far faster, while asymmetric math securely establishes the shared key
explain: TLS uses a hybrid design: asymmetric cryptography establishes or wraps a session key, then a fast symmetric cipher such as AES encrypts the traffic.

q: What does a digital signature on an email or document provide?
options: Encryption of the message or document content
Spam filtering for the recipient's mailbox
Authentication of the sender and integrity of the content, plus non-repudiation
Faster delivery of the signed message
explain: A signature hashes the content and encrypts the hash with the sender's private key; anyone can verify it with the public key, but the content is not encrypted by signing alone.

q: What is S/MIME used for?
options: Speeding up delivery between mail servers
Signing and encrypting email messages using certificates
Blocking all attachments in incoming email
Translating emails into other languages
explain: S/MIME provides end-to-end email signing and encryption based on X.509 certificates.

q: Why is a hardware security key, such as a FIDO2 USB key, phishing-resistant?
options: It performs cryptographic authentication bound to the site's origin and requires physical presence
It types the user's password into websites for them
It stores the user's passwords in a cloud vault
It works with any website password the user has
explain: A security key performs origin-bound cryptographic authentication and requires physical presence, so it cannot be tricked into authenticating a fake domain like an OTP code can.

q: How does a SIM swapping attack target a victim?
options: It clones the phone's screen to another device
It installs spyware from the phone's app store
It requires stealing the victim's physical SIM only
It convinces the carrier to move the victim's number to the attacker's SIM, hijacking SMS codes and calls
explain: SIM swapping moves the victim's number to a SIM the attacker controls, defeating SMS-based MFA; carrier account PINs and app-based MFA mitigate it.

q: How is an evil twin attack best defeated for corporate Wi-Fi users?
options: By choosing the access point with the strongest signal
By disabling encryption on the client connection
By validating the RADIUS server's certificate on the client and using EAP-TLS or PEAP with strict checks
By sharing the pre-shared key as widely as possible
explain: If clients strictly validate the authentication server's certificate, a rogue evil-twin AP cannot complete the handshake or harvest credentials.

q: What is Bluetooth bluejacking?
options: Stealing contacts from a phone over Bluetooth
Sending unsolicited messages to nearby Bluetooth devices, unlike bluesnarfing, which steals data
Jamming all Bluetooth signals in an area
Pairing without consent to play audio aloud
explain: Bluejacking is sending unwanted messages to nearby devices; bluesnarfing is unauthorized data extraction and bluebugging is taking control of a device.

q: Why are Faraday bags or cages used in forensics and security?
options: They block all radio signals to and from a device, preventing remote wipe or tracking
They charge seized devices more quickly
They cool overheating phones during imaging
They amplify Wi-Fi signals for examiners
explain: Faraday shielding isolates a device from cellular, Wi-Fi, and Bluetooth signals, preventing remote wipe or location tracking until examination.

q: How do privacy screens (polarizing filters) mitigate risk?
options: They prevent screen burn-in on the display
They reduce blue light damage to the eyes
They reduce glare from windows and lighting
They stop shoulder surfing by narrowing the display's viewing angle
explain: Privacy filters make off-angle viewing nearly impossible, protecting against shoulder surfing and visual hacking in public spaces.

q: What does secure pull printing (badge or PIN release) prevent?
options: Paper jams in high-volume print queues
Theft of toner cartridges from the device
Sensitive documents sitting unclaimed in the output tray
Double-sided printing on secure documents
explain: Pull printing holds jobs until the owner authenticates at the device, so sensitive pages do not sit unclaimed in the output tray.

q: Why does disabling AutoRun/AutoPlay for removable media reduce infections?
options: USB drives transfer files faster with it off
Malware on USB media cannot execute automatically when the media is inserted
Files cannot be copied from the media at all
The removable media is encrypted automatically
explain: AutoRun worms propagated by executing automatically on insertion; disabling auto-execution breaks that infection path.

q: Why is application allowlisting stronger than blocklisting?
options: Only approved software can run; everything unknown is denied by default
It needs no maintenance once it is configured
It allows all free software to run automatically
It scans approved software faster than a blocklist
explain: Allowlisting is deny-by-default: only approved software runs, so even never-before-seen malware has no path to execute.

q: What behaviors do Attack Surface Reduction (ASR) rules in Defender target?
options: Slow boot times caused by startup apps
Printer discovery traffic on the network
Changes to screen brightness settings
Office apps creating child processes or executables, and scripts obfuscating code
explain: ASR rules block specific techniques malware abuses inside legitimate apps, such as Office spawning child processes, rather than relying on signatures alone.

q: What are a TPM's Platform Configuration Registers (PCRs) used for in measured boot?
options: Holding the user's sign-in password
Accelerating disk encryption operations
Storing hashes of boot components so tampering with the boot chain is detectable
Replacing the Secure Boot feature entirely
explain: Each boot stage extends the PCRs with measurements of boot components; BitLocker can seal keys to the expected PCR values so tampering is detected.

q: What is the purpose of Secure Boot's revocation database (dbx)?
options: To store certificates belonging to users
To block known-bad or vulnerable bootloaders and signatures that were previously trusted
To speed up the system booting process
To list all applications installed on the PC
explain: The dbx database revokes signatures of bootloaders found to be vulnerable, preventing them from loading even though they were once trusted.

q: How does Windows Hello for Business replace passwords?
options: With asymmetric key pairs protected by the TPM and unlocked by PIN or biometrics, authenticating to AD or Azure AD
With a longer password policy for all users
With SMS codes sent to the user's phone
With security questions the user answers at sign-in
explain: Hello for Business provisions device-bound asymmetric keys protected by the TPM, giving phishing-resistant sign-on unlocked by a PIN or biometrics.

q: How does LSA protection (RunAsPPL) help secure Windows?
options: It blocks phishing emails from reaching users
It prevents USB drives from infecting the PC
It forces users to choose stronger passwords
It prevents credential theft tools from reading LSASS process memory
explain: Running LSASS as a protected process (RunAsPPL) blocks the memory reads and code injection that credential-dumping tools rely on.

q: What does Event ID 4625 in the Windows Security log record?
options: A successful logon to the system
A password change for a user account
A failed logon attempt, including the source and reason
The installation of a new Windows service
explain: Event 4625 records failed logon attempts with source and reason, providing the raw data for detecting brute force and password spraying.

q: How does a worm differ from a virus?
options: A worm cannot harm files on a system
A worm only spreads by infecting USB drives
A worm requires a macro to run before spreading
A worm spreads between systems by itself over the network without a host file or user action
explain: Worms self-propagate across networks, often through vulnerabilities, while viruses attach to host files and typically need user action to spread.

q: What is a logic bomb?
options: Malware that encrypts files for ransom
Malware that records the user's keystrokes
Malware that executes its payload when a specific condition or date is met
Malware that spreads by email automatically
explain: A logic bomb stays dormant until a specific condition or date triggers its payload, a pattern classically associated with insider attacks.

q: What does a Remote Access Trojan (RAT) give an attacker?
options: Only a one-time pop-up on the victim's screen
Ongoing remote control of the infected machine as if they were the user
Faster internet access through the victim's PC
A backup copy of the victim's Windows registry
explain: A RAT provides persistent interactive access to the infected machine, including screen, files, camera, and command execution.

q: Why is fileless malware hard to detect?
options: It lives in memory and abuses legitimate tools such as PowerShell and WMI instead of dropping files to disk
It uses stronger encryption than other malware
It hides exclusively inside photo files
It needs no network connection to operate
explain: Fileless malware lives off the land in memory using signed system tools, evading antivirus that primarily scans files on disk.

q: How do double-extortion ransomware groups increase pressure on victims?
options: They demand payment in two different cryptocurrencies
They encrypt the victim's files twice
They delete the victim's backups and nothing else
They steal data first and threaten to publish it, in addition to encrypting it
explain: In double extortion, attackers exfiltrate data and threaten to leak it as well as encrypting it, so even victims with good backups face pressure to pay.

q: How does a macro virus spread primarily?
options: Through BIOS updates applied to systems
Through network cables between computers
Through malicious macros embedded in Office documents shared between users
Through printer drivers installed on PCs
explain: Macro malware rides inside Office documents; modern Office versions block macros in internet-sourced documents by default.

q: Why is a kernel-level rootkit especially dangerous?
options: It cannot be removed by rebooting the system only
It runs with the highest privileges and can hide processes, files, and itself from the OS and security tools
It uses no memory while it is running
It only affects web browsers on the system
explain: A kernel rootkit runs with the highest privileges and can subvert the very tools used to detect it, so offline scans or a rebuild are the reliable cure.

q: What trait do spyware and keyloggers share?
options: They covertly monitor user activity and exfiltrate the collected information
They encrypt the drive and demand payment
They display ransom notes on the screen
They spread to other PCs automatically
explain: Spyware and keyloggers are surveillance tools that secretly monitor activity and send what they collect to an attacker.

q: How does spear phishing differ from ordinary phishing?
options: It is delivered only by SMS messages
It never contains links or attachments
It always comes from inside the company
It is targeted at a specific person or organization using researched personal details
explain: Spear phishing uses researched details about a specific target, making it far more convincing; whaling is the variant aimed at senior executives.

q: What does Business Email Compromise (BEC) typically involve?
options: Installing ransomware through an attachment
A DDoS attack against the mail server
Impersonating an executive or vendor to trick staff into wiring money or changing payment details
Stealing the company's logo for a website
explain: BEC relies on authority and plausible context, often from lookalike domains or compromised mailboxes, rather than on malware.

q: What does a watering hole attack compromise?
options: The office coffee machine's network settings
A legitimate website frequented by the target group, infecting its visitors
A DNS registrar and nothing else
The passwords for public Wi-Fi networks
explain: In a watering hole attack, attackers compromise a site the target group trusts and wait for victims to visit it.

q: How does typosquatting profit an attacker?
options: Registering misspelled versions of popular domains to catch mistyped visits for ads, phishing, or malware
Stealing the real domain's DNS records directly
Squatting on trademarks through court filings
Redirecting the company's email to the attacker
explain: Users who mistype a URL land on the attacker's lookalike typosquatted site, which may serve ads, phishing pages, or malware.

q: How does pharming redirect victims to fake sites?
options: By sending phishing emails more quickly
By registering misspelled typo domains
By exploiting the browser's autofill feature
By poisoning DNS resolution or the hosts file so a correct URL resolves to the attacker's server
explain: Pharming poisons DNS or the hosts file, so it works even when the user types the correct address, unlike a phishing link.

q: Vishing is social engineering conducted through which channel?
options: Video deepfakes and nothing else
Text messages sent to the victim
Voice phone calls
Fake websites hosted by the attacker
explain: Vishing is voice phishing, including help-desk impersonation and executive fraud calls; SMS-based phishing is called smishing.

q: Why does the social engineering principle of authority work?
options: Everyone likes receiving free gifts
People comply with requests that appear to come from someone in charge, such as an executive, IT, or law enforcement
Attackers using authority are always polite
Company policies require employees to comply
explain: Authority is one of the persuasion principles attackers exploit: requests that appear to come from someone in charge are obeyed with less questioning.

q: How does tailgating differ from piggybacking?
options: It follows an authorized person through a secure door without their knowledge or consent
It requires the employee to knowingly hold the door
It uses a cloned badge to enter the building
It happens only in parking lots and garages
explain: In tailgating the authorized person is unaware; in piggybacking they knowingly let the other person in. Both defeat badge systems.

q: Why is dumpster diving a security concern?
options: Trash attracts pests to the building
It violates local recycling rules
It is only a facilities management issue
Discarded documents and media can reveal passwords, org charts, and sensitive data
explain: Discarded paperwork and media are an intelligence source, which is why shredding and media destruction policies exist.

q: What is pretexting best described as?
options: Guessing passwords in a systematic way
Sending bulk spam to many recipients
Inventing a fabricated scenario to manipulate a victim into divulging information or access
Cloning a legitimate website page for page
explain: Pretexting is building a believable cover story (a pretext) that makes a malicious request feel legitimate to the victim.

q: What characterizes an Advanced Persistent Threat (APT)?
options: A teenager defacing websites for attention
A well-resourced actor maintaining stealthy, long-term access to pursue specific objectives
A one-day ransomware outbreak across a company
Automated vulnerability scans run against a network
explain: APTs are typically well-resourced, often nation-state, actors that prioritize stealth and long-term persistence over quick wins.

q: Which of the following are examples of Indicators of Compromise (IOCs)?
options: Known malicious file hashes, domains, and IP addresses from threat intelligence
Employee badge numbers issued by facilities
IP addresses assigned to office printers
Software license keys purchased by the company
explain: IOCs such as malicious hashes, domains, and IPs from threat intelligence feed detection tools so known-bad artifacts are flagged across the environment.

q: What does detonating a suspicious file in a sandbox mean?
options: Deleting the file immediately without analysis
Emailing the file to all staff for awareness
Running the file on the CEO's PC to test it
Executing it in an isolated analysis environment to observe its behavior safely
explain: A sandbox executes a suspicious file in isolation so its behavior can be observed without risking production systems.

q: What do DMARC policies of p=quarantine or p=reject instruct receiving servers to do?
options: Encrypt all inbound mail for the domain
Forward failing mail to the postmaster
Dispose of mail that fails SPF/DKIM alignment checks for the domain
Accept all mail claiming to be from the domain
explain: DMARC turns SPF and DKIM alignment results into enforceable handling, so mail failing the checks is quarantined or rejected, stopping direct domain spoofing.

q: How does DKIM protect email?
options: It encrypts the message body for the recipient
It adds a cryptographic signature with the sending domain's private key that receivers verify via DNS
It checks only the sending server's IP address
It blocks all attachments in signed messages
explain: DKIM signs messages with the sending domain's private key and receivers verify the signature via DNS, proving authorization and integrity, not confidentiality.

q: How does an 'External' warning banner on inbound email help users?
options: It flags messages that originated outside the organization so impersonation attempts stand out
It blocks all external mail from being delivered
It encrypts replies sent to external addresses
It translates messages written in foreign languages
explain: An external banner makes display-name spoofing of executives stand out, though it works best combined with user training.

q: How does URL rewriting in a secure email gateway protect users?
options: It shortens all links to make emails cleaner
It removes links from email entirely
It translates links into another language
It rewrites links so clicks are re-checked for safety at the moment of use
explain: Time-of-click protection re-checks a URL when it is clicked, catching links that were weaponized after the message was delivered.

q: When does display name spoofing succeed against email users?
options: When users read mail in mobile apps with small headers
When users have MFA enabled on their accounts
When users trust the friendly From name without checking the actual email address or domain
When users read mail in plain text format
explain: Attackers set the display name to an executive's name while using an unrelated address; checking the actual domain defeats the trick.

q: What does a help-desk social engineering (vishing) call often try to get a technician to do?
