options: Reboot a server during business hours
Reset a password or MFA enrollment without properly verifying the caller's identity
Order new hardware for the caller urgently
Update the company phone directory listing
explain: Attackers target help desks to reset passwords or MFA without proper identity verification; strict callback and ID checks are the defense.

q: When is security awareness training most effective?
options: It is ongoing, role-relevant, and paired with easy reporting such as a phish report button rather than blame
It is delivered as a single annual video for all staff
It focuses on punishing employees who click phishing links
It is provided only to IT staff members
explain: Ongoing, relevant training that rewards reporting raises detection rates, while shame-based programs drive incidents underground.

q: Why is shadow IT a security risk?
options: It makes the corporate network run faster
Employees use it to buy better tools than IT provides
It reduces the number of help-desk tickets
Unsanctioned apps and services hold company data outside security controls and visibility
explain: Shadow IT services bypass DLP, retention, and access reviews because security teams cannot protect data they cannot see.

q: How does an insider threat differ from an external attacker?
options: An insider never has any technical skill
An insider always works completely alone
An insider already has legitimate access, making misuse harder to distinguish from normal work
An insider cannot be stopped by any policy
explain: Because insiders hold legitimate access, controls such as least privilege, monitoring, and separation of duties are used to detect and limit misuse.

q: How does separation of duties prevent fraud?
options: Everyone shares one password for a process
No single person can complete a sensitive process alone, such as creating a vendor and approving its payment
Tasks rotate to a new person every day
Managers approve their own expenses directly
explain: Splitting critical steps between people forces collusion for fraud, which is much harder and riskier to carry out.

q: Why are mandatory vacations and job rotation considered security controls?
options: They expose ongoing fraud or errors that require the perpetrator's constant presence to conceal
They improve employee morale and nothing else
They reduce the cost of training new staff
They are legally required in every workplace
explain: Fraud schemes that need daily tending tend to unravel when someone else sits in the chair during a mandatory absence or rotation.

q: What does access recertification (access review) require managers to do?
options: Reset all user passwords every quarter
Approve every login their staff make
Review firewall rules on a monthly basis
Periodically re-approve each person's access so stale permissions are removed
explain: Access reviews combat privilege creep by requiring managers to periodically confirm that each person's permissions are still needed.

q: Why does the joiner-mover-leaver process matter for security?
options: New hires need laptops on their first day
Email aliases multiply as people join
Access must change promptly at each transition, with leaver accounts disabled immediately at exit
Badges expire on a yearly cycle anyway
explain: Slow deprovisioning, especially for movers who accumulate rights and leavers whose accounts stay active, causes most orphaned-account incidents.

q: What do Data Loss Prevention (DLP) tools detect and block?
options: All files above a certain size limit
Sensitive data such as card numbers or SSNs leaving via email, web, USB, or print, based on content inspection
Encrypted traffic and nothing else
Spam messages entering the organization
explain: DLP inspects content and enforces policy on egress channels, alerting on or blocking sensitive data leaving the organization.

q: How does a purple team exercise differ from separate red and blue exercises?
options: Red (attack) and blue (defense) work together in real time, sharing findings so detection and response improve during the exercise
Only managers participate in the exercise
No actual attacks are simulated at any point
It replaces penetration testing contracts entirely
explain: Purple teaming pairs attackers and defenders in real time so findings become immediate defensive tuning instead of a report weeks later.

q: How does DNS filtering or sinkholing block malware?
options: It encrypts all DNS queries from endpoints
It changes all DNS servers to 8.8.8.8
It blocks port 53 entirely on the firewall
It prevents resolution of known malicious domains so infected hosts cannot reach command-and-control
explain: If a command-and-control domain will not resolve, malware is stranded; sinkhole logs also reveal which hosts are infected by their queries.

q: How does a reverse proxy differ from a forward proxy?
options: It hides the client's identity from servers
It is used only by web browsers on clients
It sits in front of servers, presenting them to clients for load balancing, WAF, and TLS offload
It cannot inspect any traffic passing through it
explain: Forward proxies serve clients; reverse proxies sit in front of servers to publish and protect them with functions such as load balancing and TLS offload.

q: What does a Web Application Firewall (WAF) protect against?
options: DDoS attacks only, at the network layer
Application-layer attacks such as SQL injection and cross-site scripting against web apps
Email phishing sent to company users
Physical theft of the web server hardware
explain: A WAF inspects HTTP(S) requests semantically and filters malicious inputs that a network firewall would pass through.

q: What is the fundamental weakness of signature-based detection?
options: It cannot recognize new or modified malware that has no known signature
It uses too little CPU on the endpoint
It requires internet access at all times
It only works on Windows operating systems
explain: Zero-day and polymorphic malware evade signature matching, which is why behavioral and EDR layers are added to endpoint protection.

q: What does behavioral or heuristic analysis in modern endpoint protection watch for?
options: File sizes of executables and nothing else
The typing speed of the signed-in user
Screen brightness patterns on the display
Suspicious actions such as mass file encryption, process injection, and credential access, rather than known file hashes
explain: Behavioral engines judge malware by what it does, forming the basis of EDR and XDR detection of novel threats.

q: How does EDR differ from traditional antivirus?
options: It only scans files when a user requests it
It cannot detect ransomware activity at all
It continuously records endpoint activity for investigation and can isolate hosts and roll back changes
It works without an agent on the endpoint
explain: EDR assumes breach: continuous telemetry, threat hunting, host isolation, and remediation are its core value beyond signature scanning.

q: What is a SIEM's core job?
options: To replace all firewalls in the environment
To collect logs from across the environment, correlate events, and alert on patterns no single source would reveal
To back up collected logs to tape storage
To block spam before it reaches mailboxes
explain: A SIEM correlates scattered logs, such as a failed logon in one place and a VPN login elsewhere, into detectable incidents.

q: How do SOAR platforms extend a security operations center?
options: They automate response playbooks such as enrich, isolate, and ticket to speed analyst workflows
They design network diagrams for the SOC
They order hardware for security projects
They write firmware for firewall appliances
explain: Security Orchestration, Automation and Response (SOAR) reduces manual toil in triage and containment by automating playbook steps.

q: When are threat intelligence feeds most useful?
options: When they are as long as possible
When they are read only once a year
When they are kept secret from the SOC
When they are actionable: mapped to the organization's environment and fed into detection and blocking tools
explain: Intelligence only has value when it changes a control, feeding automated enforcement or threat-hunting hypotheses.

q: What does a responsible bug bounty program give an organization?
options: Legal immunity for attackers of any kind
Crowdsourced vulnerability discovery from vetted external researchers, paid per valid finding within a defined scope and rules of engagement
A guarantee of zero vulnerabilities in its systems
Free penetration tests with no scope limits
explain: Defined scope, rules of engagement, and safe-harbor terms are what separate legitimate bounty research from attacks.

q: What does an implicit deny at the end of a firewall ACL mean?
options: All traffic is logged twice by the firewall
The firewall fails open when rules are exhausted
Only the last rule in the ACL matters
Any traffic not explicitly permitted is dropped
explain: Default-deny posture means rules permit known-good traffic and everything else hits the implicit deny at the end of the ACL.

q: What do egress filtering controls do?
options: Filter only inbound spam for mail servers
Control wireless signal strength on APs
Control outbound traffic, blocking exfiltration channels and unauthorized services leaving the network
Control which users can access printers
explain: Restricting what can leave the network, by port and destination, blunts command-and-control callbacks and data theft.

q: How does a stateful firewall improve on a stateless packet filter?
options: It encrypts all packets passing through it
It tracks connection state and automatically allows legitimate return traffic
It scans the contents of files for malware
It assigns IP addresses to connecting clients
explain: State tables let a stateful firewall allow replies to permitted outbound sessions without extra rules, unlike a stateless filter.

q: What does a next-generation firewall (NGFW) add over a traditional firewall?
options: Application awareness, integrated IPS, and user-identity-based rules
More Ethernet ports on the appliance
A built-in printer for security reports
Free VPN licenses that never expire
explain: NGFWs identify applications regardless of port and add integrated intrusion prevention and identity-based policy.

q: What is a Unified Threat Management (UTM) appliance aimed at?
options: Replacing all servers in an organization
Enterprise core routing and nothing else
Physical access control for buildings
Combining firewall, IPS, antivirus, content filtering, and more in one box for smaller organizations
explain: UTM trades depth for simplicity by combining many security functions in one appliance with one management console.

q: How does microsegmentation improve internal security?
options: It makes subnets smaller to increase speed
It removes all VLANs from the network
It enforces firewall policies between individual workloads inside the network, not just at the perimeter
It encrypts DNS queries and nothing else
explain: Microsegmentation applies policy to east-west traffic between workloads, limiting lateral movement after one internal system is breached.

q: How does WPA3's SAE handshake improve over WPA2-PSK?
options: It makes passwords unnecessary for Wi-Fi
It resists offline dictionary attacks against a captured handshake and provides forward secrecy
It doubles the speed of the Wi-Fi connection
It removes the need for passwords entirely
explain: SAE (Dragonfly) prevents offline brute-forcing of a captured handshake and gives each session unique keys for forward secrecy.

q: Why is WPA2-Enterprise with 802.1X preferred in companies?
options: Each user or device authenticates individually, so access can be revoked per person, unlike a shared PSK
It needs no RADIUS server to operate
It is faster than using a pre-shared key
User passwords never need to change
explain: Per-user credentials avoid the shared office Wi-Fi password problem and let access be revoked for one person at a time.

q: What can a wireless intrusion prevention system (WIPS) do?
options: Boost the signal strength of access points
Replace the RADIUS server for the network
Encrypt traffic on the wired network
Detect rogue APs and evil twins and actively deauthenticate clients connecting to them
explain: A WIPS monitors the RF environment for unauthorized wireless devices and can actively contain them by deauthenticating their clients.

q: Why should Bluetooth be disabled on secure workstations when it is unused?
options: It drains the CMOS battery on the motherboard
It conflicts with NTP time synchronization
It expands the attack surface through pairing exploits and bluesnarfing within physical proximity
It permanently slows the workstation's CPU
explain: Bluetooth proximity attacks and forgotten discoverable modes expose data, so disabling it when unused reduces the attack surface.

q: RFID badges can be cloned with cheap readers. How do high-security facilities mitigate this?
options: They issue longer badge lanyards to staff
They use encrypted smart credentials such as SEOS or DESFire plus MFA such as badge + PIN at critical doors
They print color photos on the badges
They install more badge readers at doors
explain: Legacy 125 kHz prox cards are trivially copyable; encrypted credentials and a second factor such as a PIN close the hole.

q: What does an access control vestibule (mantrap) prevent?
options: Tailgating: only one person is admitted at a time into the secured area
Power outages in the secured facility
Cloning of employee access badges
Failures of security camera systems
explain: An access control vestibule uses interlocking doors to verify a single occupant before releasing the inner door, preventing tailgating.

q: What do bollards in front of a building protect against?
options: Tailgating through the building entrance
Dumpster diving in the waste area
RFID skimming of employee badges
Vehicle ramming attacks against entrances and storefronts
explain: Bollards are rated physical barriers designed to stop vehicle-borne attacks against entrances and storefronts.

q: Why is clean-agent fire suppression used in server rooms?
options: It is cheaper than sprinkler systems to install
It doubles as cooling for the server room
It extinguishes fire without water or chemical residue that would destroy electronics
It requires no maintenance after installation
explain: Gaseous clean agents such as FM-200 or Novec suppress fire while leaving equipment intact, unlike water-based systems.

q: In a workplace context, what are Faraday cages used for?
options: Blocking heat from sensitive equipment rooms
Shielding sensitive areas or test devices from RF signals and emissions
Soundproofing rooms and nothing else
Storing magnetic tapes for long periods
explain: Faraday cages provide RF shielding that prevents wireless communication with enclosed devices and reduces emanation leakage.

q: How are air-gapped systems protected?
options: By complete physical isolation from other networks, so data moves only via controlled media
By a very strong firewall configuration
By running two antivirus products together
By hiding the network's SSID from scans
explain: Air gaps isolate the most sensitive systems from all networks; controlled media handling then becomes the main risk to manage.

q: How do immutable backups defend against ransomware?
options: They make backups complete much faster
They compress backup data more efficiently
They eliminate the need for off-site copies
They prevent backup data from being modified or deleted for a set retention period, even by admins or attackers
explain: Attackers target backups first; immutability guarantees a clean restore point survives, as in the '1 immutable' of the 3-2-1-1-0 rule.

q: What does the '0' in the 3-2-1-1-0 backup rule stand for?
options: Zero cost for the backup solution
Zero downtime guaranteed during restores
Zero errors after backup verification and testing
Zero administrators managing the backups
explain: The rule means 3 copies, on 2 media types, 1 off-site, 1 offline or immutable, and 0 errors after verification.

q: What are the NIST SP 800-88 media sanitization levels?
options: Wipe, Format, and Recycle
Clear, Purge, and Destroy, in increasing assurance for removing data from media
Low, Medium, and High
Delete, Shred, and Burn only
explain: SP 800-88 defines Clear (logical), Purge (such as degaussing or crypto-erase), and Destroy (physical), matched to media type and sensitivity.

q: Why does degaussing work on magnetic media but not on SSDs?
options: SSDs store data as electrical charges in flash cells, not as magnetic domains
SSDs are too small for degaussers to affect
Degaussers are illegal to use on SSDs
SSDs have no platters to spin down
explain: Degaussing disrupts magnetic domains, so it cannot erase flash storage; SSDs need crypto-erase or physical destruction per SP 800-88.

q: What does a certificate of destruction provide?
options: A warranty for replacement drives
A tax deduction for destroyed equipment
Encryption keys for the new replacement drive
Documented proof that specific media was sanitized or destroyed, with serial numbers, method, date, and witness
explain: A certificate of destruction completes the chain of custody with the details compliance audits require for each item of media.

q: What do data classification labels such as Public, Internal, Confidential, and Restricted drive?
options: File naming conventions and nothing else
Printer priorities for queued documents
Handling rules for encryption, sharing limits, retention, and destruction per sensitivity
Email signature formats for employees
explain: Classification tells every downstream control how to treat the data, from encryption and sharing to retention and destruction.

q: How does watermarking documents help security?
options: It encrypts the document's contents
It attributes leaks, because visible or forensic marks identify whose copy was disclosed
It prevents the document from being copied entirely
It compresses the document for distribution
explain: Per-recipient watermarks deter leaks and support investigations by identifying whose copy of a document surfaced.

q: What does rights management (IRM/DRM) on documents enforce?
options: Persistent controls such as no forwarding, expiry, and view-only, even after the file leaves the network
Antivirus scanning of document contents
Faster downloads of shared documents
Version history for document edits
explain: IRM travels with the file, extending controls such as no-forwarding and expiry beyond the network perimeter.

q: How does a password manager improve user security mainly?
options: It shares passwords with the whole team
It removes the need for MFA on accounts
It stores passwords in the browser only
It enables a unique, strong password for every account without a memorization burden
explain: Unique passwords per site neutralize credential stuffing; the vault itself is protected by a strong master password plus MFA.

q: What does current passphrase guidance favor?
options: One word plus a single digit at the end
The user's pet name with a birth year
Long, memorable phrases of four or more random words over short, complex strings
Reusing the same phrase across many sites
explain: Length dominates entropy for human-usable secrets, so long passphrases are favored; NIST guidance also drops forced periodic changes absent compromise.

q: Why are security keys and authenticator apps preferred over SMS codes?
options: SMS codes are too slow to be delivered
SMS is vulnerable to SIM swapping and number porting fraud
Phones cannot receive SMS inside offices
Authenticator apps are free to download
explain: SMS codes ride the phone network's weak identity checks and can be hijacked by SIM swapping; TOTP and hardware keys stay on the user's device.

q: What is a honeypot's value in an enterprise?
options: Any interaction with a decoy system is suspicious by definition, generating high-fidelity early-warning alerts
Hosting production backups for the business
Replacing the perimeter firewall entirely
Speeding up the internal network for users
explain: A honeypot has no legitimate users, so any interaction with it is almost never a false positive and signals an intruder early.

q: How does threat hunting differ from alert-driven monitoring?
options: It waits for the SIEM to fire an alert
It only reviews firewall logs for anomalies
It is performed once a year by auditors
It proactively searches for signs of compromise based on hypotheses, assuming attackers may already be inside
explain: Threat hunting is human-led and intelligence-driven, searching for what signatures and alerts may have missed.

q: How does a vulnerability scan differ from a penetration test?
options: A scan is illegal without permission to run
A scan tests people rather than systems
A scan automatically enumerates known vulnerabilities, while a pentest actively exploits weaknesses to prove impact
A scan takes months to complete properly
explain: Scans find potential issues at scale; penetration tests demonstrate real-world exploitability by chaining and exploiting weaknesses.

q: How is risk commonly expressed?
options: As the cost of the control alone
As likelihood multiplied by impact (threat times vulnerability in qualitative models)
As the number of firewalls deployed
As the CVSS score of a single bug
explain: Risk assessments weigh how likely an event is against how bad it would be, in order to prioritize treatment.

q: What are the four standard risk treatments?
options: Mitigate, accept, transfer (such as insurance), and avoid
Ignore, deny, blame, and delete
Patch, reboot, scan, and repeat
Encrypt everything in the environment
explain: Every identified risk receives a deliberate treatment decision — mitigate, accept, transfer, or avoid — that is documented and owned.

q: What is a compensating control?
options: A control that pays fines after an incident
A second antivirus product on the same system
An insurance policy and nothing else
An alternative safeguard used when the primary control cannot be implemented, such as extra monitoring where patching is impossible
explain: A compensating control provides equivalent protection when the primary requirement cannot be met, a concept formalized by PCI DSS.

q: What does defense in depth mean?
options: Buying the most expensive firewall available
Encrypting the same data three times
Layering independent controls so no single failure exposes the asset
Hiring more guards for the facility
explain: Defense in depth layers perimeter, segmentation, endpoint, identity, and backup controls so each catches what the others miss.

q: A password manager advertises a 'zero-knowledge' architecture. What does that mean?
options: Users need no master password for the vault
The provider can reset any vault entry for you
Passwords are stored in plaintext for speed
Vaults are encrypted and decrypted only on the user's device with keys derived from the master password, so the provider cannot read stored passwords
explain: Zero-knowledge means the provider cannot read vault contents, which is also why a forgotten master password can mean a lost vault.

q: How might an allowlist approach to USB storage work in high-security areas?
options: Device control policies permit only specific encrypted, company-issued drives by serial number or ID
USB ports are blocked physically with glue only
All drives are allowed but scanned once a month
Users' judgment is trusted for removable media
explain: Endpoint device control can allow only sanctioned encrypted drives by ID and block all other removable storage.

q: When do SmartScreen and reputation services warn users?
options: When the device battery is running low
When a chosen password is judged weak
When the display screen is dirty
When a downloaded program or site has an unknown or malicious reputation
explain: Reputation checks act as a last-moment guardrail against fresh malware and phishing sites with unknown or bad reputations.

q: Windows Defender Firewall applies different rule sets for which network locations?
options: Each individual user account on the PC
Wired versus wireless network cables
Domain, Private, and Public network locations
Daytime versus nighttime hours
explain: The firewall uses Domain, Private, and Public profiles, tightening rules automatically on untrusted Public networks.

q: What value does a host-based firewall add beyond the network firewall?
options: It scans email attachments for malware
It protects the machine on hostile networks and can control outbound connections per application
It replaces the need for patching entirely
It encrypts the workstation's disk drive
explain: A host firewall travels with the laptop, protecting it on untrusted networks and enforcing per-application egress rules.

q: How does MAC address randomization on phones protect privacy?
options: It uses rotating fake MACs for Wi-Fi probing so the device cannot be tracked across locations
It hides the device's IP address from websites
It encrypts Bluetooth connections automatically
It blocks advertisements across all apps
explain: Randomized MACs defeat tracking based on Wi-Fi probe requests; a network the phone joins may still see a consistent per-network MAC.

q: Disabling unused network services and ports on a workstation is an example of what?
options: Security through obscurity and nothing else
A backup strategy for the workstation
Load balancing across network services
Reducing the attack surface through system hardening
explain: Every listening service is a potential door; hardening closes the unneeded ones to shrink the attack surface.

q: How do banner grabs and login page warnings ('Authorized use only') support security?
options: They slow down attackers at a technical level
They encrypt the login process for users
They provide legal notice that monitoring is in effect and unauthorized access is prohibited
They hide the server version and nothing else
explain: Warning banners strengthen prosecution and set expectations that activity is monitored and unauthorized use is prohibited.

q: What do security baselines from vendors, such as Microsoft security baselines or CIS Benchmarks, provide?
options: Free software licenses for hardened systems
Pre-tested, recommended configuration standards to harden systems consistently
Custom malware samples for testing defenses
Physical security layouts for facilities
explain: Baselines encode expert consensus so systems are hardened consistently rather than hand-tuned machine by machine.

q: What does the Group Policy setting 'Password must meet complexity requirements' enforce?
options: Passwords mixing character classes and not containing the account name
Passwords that are set to never expire
Passwords of exactly eight characters in length
PIN-only logons for all user accounts
explain: Complexity requirements combine character classes with length policies; modern guidance also emphasizes length and screening against breached passwords.

q: What does a rainbow table attack use?
options: Rainbow-colored phishing pages to lure users
Precomputed chains of password hashes to reverse common passwords quickly, defeated by salting
A table of network routes on the target
Brute force with GPUs and nothing else
explain: Rainbow tables trade storage for speed in reversing hashes; a unique salt per password makes precomputation useless.

q: How does a dictionary attack differ from brute force?
options: It tries likely words, phrases, and mutations instead of every possible combination
It only attacks network shares on a LAN
It requires the password hash file to work
It is always slower than brute force attacks
explain: Dictionary attacks exploit predictable human password choices, while brute force tries every combination and succeeds only given enough time.

q: Why do pass-the-hash attacks work?
options: Hashes can be decrypted using the username
Windows stores passwords in plain text form
The hash is the same string as the username
The attacker uses a stolen NTLM hash to authenticate without knowing the plaintext password
explain: NTLM authentication accepts the hash itself as proof, so a stolen hash can be replayed; Credential Guard, LAPS, and disabling NTLM mitigate it.

q: How is MFA fatigue (push bombing) countered most directly?
options: By sending more push notifications to the user
By removing MFA from the account entirely
By number matching: the user enters digits shown on the sign-in screen into the authenticator prompt
By switching the account to SMS codes instead
explain: Number matching proves the user is present at the actual sign-in attempt, defeating blind approval of spammed push prompts.

q: How is SQL injection prevented at the application level primarily?
options: By hiding the database password from users
By parameterized queries or prepared statements that keep user input separate from SQL code
By using longer table names in the database
By blocking the word SELECT everywhere in input
explain: Parameterization is the structural fix for SQL injection because input can never be interpreted as SQL code; a WAF is only a compensating layer.

q: What does cross-site scripting (XSS) let an attacker do?
options: Run malicious scripts in victims' browsers in the context of a vulnerable site
Inject SQL queries directly into a database
Steal the server's private key directly
Bypass the network firewall entirely
explain: XSS abuses a site's trust in user input to run scripts in victims' browsers; output encoding and Content Security Policy are the defenses.

q: What does cross-site request forgery (CSRF) trick a browser into doing?
options: Revealing its stored passwords to a site
Installing a rootkit on the user's machine
Mining cryptocurrency for the attacker
Submitting an unwanted request to a site where the user is already authenticated
explain: The target site sees a valid session cookie on the forged request; anti-CSRF tokens and SameSite cookies are the standard mitigations.

q: What do directory (path) traversal attacks use sequences such as ../ to do?
options: List the site's directory for search engines
Speed up file downloads from the server
Escape the web root and access files elsewhere on the server
Enumerate users in Active Directory
explain: Poor input sanitization in traversal attacks lets attackers reach configuration files and credentials outside the intended web folder.

q: What do privilege escalation vulnerabilities allow an attacker to do?
options: Reset any user's password by email request
Move from a low-privilege account to admin, SYSTEM, or root control
Encrypt the disk of the target system
Spoof the MAC address of the network card
explain: Vertical privilege escalation gains higher rights on a system, distinct from lateral movement to other machines at the same privilege level.

q: What is a zero-day vulnerability?
options: One that is exploited before the vendor has released a patch, so the vendor has had zero days to fix it
One that was discovered earlier today
One that affects only old, unsupported systems
One that cannot be exploited remotely at all
explain: Zero-days justify defense in depth and virtual patching with IPS or WAF rules while the vendor develops a fix.

q: How do software supply-chain attacks compromise targets?
options: By cutting the vendor's power supply
By stealing the vendor's office laptops
By phishing the vendor's customers only
By inserting malicious code into a legitimate vendor's software or update that customers trust and install
explain: Supply-chain attacks turn a trusted update channel into the delivery mechanism, which is why code signing and verification matter.

q: How is session hijacking via cookie theft mitigated?
options: By making session cookies longer strings
By storing session IDs in the URL instead
By HttpOnly and Secure cookie flags, TLS everywhere, and short session lifetimes with re-authentication for sensitive actions
By disabling TLS on the web application
explain: HttpOnly and Secure flags, TLS, and short session lifetimes limit the usefulness of a stolen session cookie.

q: How does an IMSI catcher (cell-site simulator or 'stingray') attack mobile users?
options: It clones the SIM card physically in a shop
It pretends to be a cell tower so phones connect to it, enabling interception and location tracking
It sends fake SMS messages to subscribers
It jams all cellular bands in an area
explain: An IMSI catcher forces phones to connect to it, often with downgrades to weaker protocols; modern 4G/5G mutual authentication raises the bar.

q: What is the risk known as juice jacking?
options: A public USB charging port or cable is modified to steal data or install malware, which a USB data blocker prevents
Charging too fast damages phone batteries
Airports charge fees for using power outlets
USB cables wear out from repeated public use
explain: Juice jacking abuses the data lines of public USB charging; charge-only adapters pass power without data, neutralizing the attack.

q: Quishing is phishing delivered through what?
options: Voice calls impersonating a help desk
SMS messages sent to mobile phones
Fake invoices sent to accounting staff
QR codes that lead to credential-harvesting sites, often bypassing email link scanning
explain: QR codes hide the destination URL from users and some filters, so users should preview where a code leads before opening it.

q: What security trade-off do split-tunnel VPN configurations carry?
options: The VPN takes twice as long to connect
No encryption is used on the tunnel at all
Only work traffic goes through the tunnel; the user's other internet traffic bypasses corporate inspection and controls
Users cannot reach the internet while connected
explain: Split tunneling saves bandwidth but leaves a bridge between the internet and the corporate network on the same machine.

q: What is the most important hardening step for a home-office router?
options: Hiding the SSID and nothing else
Changing the default admin password, updating firmware, and using WPA2-AES or WPA3 with a strong passphrase while disabling WPS and remote admin
Setting the transmit power to maximum
Renaming the network to the company name
explain: Default credentials and unpatched firmware are the top home-router compromises, and WPS PIN mode is notoriously weak.

q: What is the safest practice for sensitive work on public Wi-Fi?
options: Avoid it, or use a trusted VPN and verify the exact network name with staff; prefer cellular when possible
Connect to the strongest open signal available
Disable the firewall to improve connection speed
Turn off OS updates while using the network
explain: Open networks allow sniffing and evil twins; a VPN encrypts traffic beyond the local segment and cellular avoids the shared network entirely.

q: How do modern mobile OS runtime permissions improve security?
options: They grant all permissions at install permanently
They remove the settings app from the phone
They encrypt the app store and its downloads
They ask users to grant sensitive permissions such as location, camera, and contacts per app at first use, revocable anytime
explain: Per-app, revocable runtime permissions replaced the old all-or-nothing install-time model for sensitive data and sensors.

q: What do Mobile Threat Defense (MTD) apps add?
options: Extra battery life for managed phones
Free data plans for enrolled devices
On-device detection of malicious apps, risky networks, and OS tampering beyond basic MDM controls
A second app store for company applications
explain: MTD is the mobile analog of endpoint protection and feeds risk signals into conditional access decisions.

q: What does always-on VPN on a managed phone ensure?
options: The battery lasts longer during the workday
All traffic is tunneled through the corporate VPN before reaching the internet, with connections blocked if the tunnel drops
Users can bypass geographic restrictions easily
Wi-Fi calling works better on the device
explain: Always-on VPN with lockdown behavior prevents traffic leaking outside the tunnel if the VPN connection fails.

q: How does Android's Private DNS feature (DNS over TLS) protect mobile users?
options: It encrypts DNS queries to a chosen resolver so local networks cannot snoop or tamper with them
It changes the device's IP address regularly
It blocks all advertisements system-wide
It speeds up 5G connections on the phone
explain: Encrypted DNS (DoT or DoH) closes the plain-text DNS snooping and tampering hole on untrusted networks.

q: What is a laptop cable lock a deterrent against?
options: Data theft over the corporate network
An insider copying files to USB media
Water damage in public workspaces
Opportunistic physical theft (snatch-and-grab) in public or shared spaces
explain: A cable lock using the Kensington slot delays rather than defeats a determined thief, but it stops walk-away thefts.

q: Why are cross-cut (micro-cut) shredders preferred over strip-cut for sensitive documents?
options: They are quieter than strip-cut shredders
They never jam on sensitive documents
They reduce paper to much smaller particles that are impractical to reconstruct
They shred documents faster than strip-cut models
explain: Higher DIN security levels such as P-4 specify small particle sizes that make reconstruction of confidential material impractical.

q: What does a clean desk policy require?
options: Desks to be cleaned daily by janitorial staff
Sensitive documents and media to be locked away when unattended, with screens locked
No personal items to be kept at work
All paper to be banned from the workplace
explain: Clean desk and clear screen practices reduce opportunistic information theft in offices and home workspaces.

q: What does visitor management best practice in secure facilities include?
options: Signing in, identity verification, visible badges, and escorting visitors at all times in sensitive areas
Letting visitors roam if they look professional
Badges only for guests staying overnight
No records kept of visitor activity
explain: Sign-in logs, verified identity, visible badges, and escorts close the social-engineering door that open offices create.

q: What do passive infrared (PIR) sensors detect to identify intruders?
options: Sound waves moving through the room
Magnetic fields around door frames
Light levels and changes in brightness only
Changes in infrared heat signatures as body heat moves across zones
explain: PIR sensors detect moving body heat and are the standard motion detector in alarm systems and automatic lighting.

q: How does reviewing door access logs after an incident help investigators?
options: It unlocks doors remotely for responders
It resets all badges in the affected area
It reconstructs who badged into which areas and when, correlating with camera footage
It changes the alarm code for the building
explain: Badge logs often provide the timeline backbone of a physical incident investigation when correlated with camera footage.

q: What does Tamper Protection in Windows Security prevent?
options: Users from changing the desktop wallpaper
Malware or rogue scripts from disabling Defender settings such as real-time protection
Windows Update from running on the device
Admins from ever changing Defender settings
explain: With Tamper Protection on, Defender's security settings can only be changed through proper channels, not by malware or scripts.

q: What does cloud-delivered protection in Microsoft Defender Antivirus provide?
options: Near-instant protection against newly discovered malware via cloud lookups, complementing local signatures
Free cloud storage for quarantined files
Faster file downloads from the internet
Automatic backups of the user's documents
explain: Cloud-delivered protection shortens the gap between a new threat's discovery and protection on the client.

q: What does network protection, a Microsoft Defender feature, block?
options: All HTTPS traffic from applications
Windows Update connections to Microsoft
Local file shares on the home network
Connections to malicious or phishing domains and low-reputation sites at the network level
explain: Network protection extends SmartScreen-style reputation checks beyond the browser to other apps and processes.

q: What does PUA protection in Windows guard against?
options: All free software installed by the user
Applications from the Microsoft Store only
Potentially unwanted applications such as adware, bundleware, and cryptominers that are not strictly malware
Open-source software and nothing else
explain: Potentially unwanted applications degrade performance and privacy without crossing the malware line; blocking them is a policy choice.

q: What do Data Execution Prevention (DEP) and Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR) do to make exploitation harder?
options: Encrypt the entire system drive so stored data cannot be read without a key
Prevent code execution from data pages and randomize memory layout to make exploitation unreliable
Scan files and running processes for known malware signatures at startup
Compress inactive memory pages to free RAM for foreground applications
explain: DEP marks data pages as non-executable, and ASLR randomizes memory addresses, so memory-corruption exploits become unreliable.

q: How does Network Level Authentication (NLA) improve the security of Remote Desktop?
options: Authenticating the user before a full remote session is created, reducing the server's exposed attack surface
Removing the need for passwords by allowing anonymous remote logons
Encrypting clipboard contents while leaving the logon screen exposed to all users
Speeding up logons only, with no change to authentication or exposure
explain: NLA uses CredSSP to authenticate users before the logon session is created, so unauthenticated users never reach the logon screen.

q: Why is exposing Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) directly to the internet considered dangerous?
options: Because RDP traffic uses too much bandwidth for a typical internet connection
Because RDP traffic cannot be encrypted even when it is configured correctly
Because only one user can connect, so attackers can easily lock out administrators
Because it is constantly brute-forced and targeted by exploits and belongs behind a VPN or RD Gateway with MFA
explain: Internet bots scan port 3389 continuously for brute-force and exploit attempts, so RDP should sit behind a VPN or RD Gateway with MFA.

q: Which set of actions correctly hardens SSH access on a Linux server?
options: Enabling Telnet as a fallback remote-access method so administrators can still log in if SSH fails
Sharing the root password among administrators so emergency access never depends on a single person
Using key-only authentication, disabling direct root login, limiting allowed users, and optionally rate-limiting with fail2ban
Allowing password authentication from any address with no failed-attempt limits or lockout policy applied
explain: SSH keys, disabled direct root login, and restricted users close the brute-force path that password authentication leaves open.

q: How does fail2ban protect Linux services against brute-force attacks?
options: By encrypting authentication logs so failed logon attempts cannot be inspected by attackers or admins
By monitoring logs for repeated authentication failures and temporarily banning offending IPs via the firewall
By resetting user passwords automatically after several failed logons and emailing the new credentials
By blocking all foreign IP addresses permanently at the firewall regardless of failed logon attempts
explain: Fail2ban watches service logs and turns repeated failures into automatic, time-limited firewall bans.

q: What does macOS System Integrity Protection (SIP) prevent?
options: Even root from modifying critical system files and processes, limiting rootkit persistence
Applications from the App Store from accessing the user's documents folder
Users from changing desktop settings such as the wallpaper image
Time Machine from backing up protected system volumes and files
explain: SIP protects core macOS files and processes even from root, which limits rootkit persistence.

q: What is XProtect in macOS?
options: A stateful firewall that filters inbound and outbound network traffic
A backup tool that creates bootable clones of the system volume
A VPN client that tunnels traffic through Apple's relay servers
Signature-based malware detection and remediation that updates silently in the background
explain: XProtect, together with Gatekeeper and MRT, provides Apple's built-in signature-based anti-malware protection.

q: How should browser extensions be managed to reduce their security risk?
options: Install as many extensions as possible so users can compare their behavior
Sideload extensions from internal file shares instead of official stores
Allow only vetted extensions from official stores and review the permissions each one requests
Grant every permission an extension requests so it functions without prompts
explain: Extensions run with broad page access, so only vetted extensions with reviewed permissions should be allowed.

q: What does enabling Secure DNS (DNS over HTTPS) in a browser do?
options: Forces every website the browser visits to load over HTTPS
Encrypts DNS lookups between the browser and resolver, hiding them from the local network
Blocks all trackers and advertising content automatically in every site
Replaces the need for a VPN for all browser and application traffic
explain: DNS over HTTPS encrypts name resolution between the browser and its resolver, hiding lookups from the local network.

q: What risk does restricting the local Administrators group through Group Policy defend against?
options: Users and malware running with standing local admin rights and using them for lateral movement
Slow logons caused by users processing too many group memberships when they sign in to the domain
Printer failures caused by restricted driver installation rights on shared workstation computers
Disk fragmentation caused by unrestricted user file writes across many local workstation drives
explain: Removing everyday users from local Administrators is a high-value hardening step because standing admin rights aid malware and lateral movement.

q: How should a Windows Firewall rule that allows an application be scoped?
options: Allow all profiles and all remote addresses by default for reliability
Disable the firewall instead of creating a narrow exception rule
Allow the entire internet permanently so the application never breaks
Limit the rule to the needed profile and, where possible, specific remote IPs, subnets, and ports
explain: Least-privilege firewall rules limited by profile, address, and port reduce exposure compared with allow-any rules.

q: Why do change and configuration baselines help protect security?
options: Because baselined systems never need to be patched again afterward
Because baselined systems prevent users from installing local printers
Because deviations from a known-good hardened configuration become visible and investigable
Because baselined systems make security logging unnecessary to review
explain: Baseline drift detection makes configuration attacks and mistakes visible so they can be investigated.

q: What is the purpose of using a DMZ jump box (jump server) for administration?
options: To speed up Remote Desktop by caching sessions closer to administrators
To force all admin access to internal systems through one hardened, logged chokepoint
To bypass MFA checks for administrators connecting from the DMZ
To host the company website separately from internal web servers
explain: A jump host centralizes privileged access through one hardened, monitored chokepoint.

q: A Windows PC has become slow to boot over several months. What is the most effective first diagnostic step?
options: Reinstalling Windows immediately before collecting any diagnostic evidence
Defragmenting the registry with a third-party registry cleaner tool
Checking Task Manager's Startup tab and using a clean-boot comparison to find heavy auto-start items
Installing a second antivirus product to scan during the boot process
explain: Boot slowdowns usually accumulate from auto-start apps and services, and the Startup tab plus clean boot isolate them.

q: A user's Windows PIN shows 'This option is currently unavailable.' What is a common repair for this problem?
options: Reinstalling Windows to rebuild all Windows Hello credentials at once
Deleting the Ngc folder contents in an admin or Safe Mode context and setting up the PIN again
Formatting the system drive and restoring the user's files from backup
Disabling the TPM permanently so Windows Hello stops requiring it
explain: Corrupted Ngc container data breaks Windows Hello credentials, and clearing it lets Windows rebuild the PIN store.

q: A fingerprint reader disappears from sign-in options after an update. Beyond checking the driver, what should a technician check?
options: That the Windows Biometric Service is running on the computer
That the Recycle Bin has been emptied after the update completed
That the printer spooler service is running without errors
That the Xbox Game Bar service is enabled for sign-in options
explain: Windows Hello biometrics depend on the Windows Biometric Service, and a stopped service removes the sign-in option.

q: Sound works in most applications but one game is silent. Which setting is most likely responsible?
options: The monitor's built-in speakers are muted in its on-screen menu while other apps use another device
An outdated GPU driver is preventing the game from initializing its audio rendering pipeline stage
A failing CMOS battery is resetting the saved audio device settings each time the computer shuts down
Per-app volume or output device settings in Volume Mixer, or the app's exclusive-mode setting
explain: Windows remembers per-app volume levels and output devices, so App volume and device preferences should be checked first.

q: A Bluetooth headset pairs successfully but never connects for audio. What is the standard fix sequence?
options: Replace the headset battery with a larger-capacity battery pack
Reinstall Windows to rebuild the entire Bluetooth driver stack
Remove the device, re-pair it, and confirm the Bluetooth Support Service is running
Disable Wi-Fi permanently because it interferes with Bluetooth audio
explain: Stale pairings corrupt the connection profile, and removing and re-pairing the device rebuilds it.

q: Wi-Fi disconnects every time a laptop sleeps or the lid closes and takes a minute to return. What is a quick fix for this behavior?
options: Disable the Windows Firewall profile for the wireless network so reconnect traffic is never inspected
In Device Manager, uncheck 'Allow the computer to turn off this device to save power' for the wireless adapter
Set a static IP address permanently on the wireless adapter so the address survives every sleep cycle
Replace the wireless router with a newer model whose beacon timing wakes sleeping laptop adapters sooner
explain: Aggressive adapter power management can power down the radio during sleep transitions, causing slow reconnection.

q: A network printer shows 'Offline' in Windows although it is powered on and pingable. What is a classic fix for this problem?
options: In the printer's port settings, uncheck 'SNMP Status Enabled' or set the correct SNMP community
Reinstall Windows to rebuild the print queue, its port configuration, and the spooler service database
Replace the printer's network cable with a longer cable run to reduce packet loss to the print device
Delete all queued print jobs permanently from every user's queue to reset the printer's offline state
explain: Incorrect SNMP status replies make Windows mark a queue offline, and disabling SNMP status monitoring corrects it.

q: Users suddenly get error 0x0000011b when connecting to a shared printer after a Windows security update. What is the cause?
options: The shared printer has run out of paper in its main tray, so the server rejects new authenticated connections
DNS on the client computers has stopped resolving the print server's name to its current IP address value
The print spooler on the server has exhausted its allocated memory while processing the shared print queue
Hardened RPC and point-and-print authentication changes; fully patch the print server or apply the documented registry mitigation
explain: PrintNightmare-era patches changed spooler RPC authentication, which broke older print servers until they were fully patched or configured.

q: The default printer keeps changing to the last-used printer. Which setting should be disabled to stop this?
options: Hardware acceleration for printing in the advanced printer settings
Fast Startup in the Windows power options control panel
'Let Windows manage my default printer' in printer settings
Hibernate in the current Windows power plan configuration
explain: The 'Let Windows manage my default printer' feature sets the default to the most recently used printer.

q: Shared printer connections keep prompting some users for credentials after policy hardening. Which area is most likely responsible?
options: The printer's internal clock is out of sync with the print server, so Kerberos tickets are rejected at logon
Guest and insecure logon restrictions, such as SMB signing and guest authentication blocks, between client and print host
The paper size in the shared printer's default settings conflicts with the client's regional print settings
The users' cached credentials for the print host were cleared by the hardening policy's credential rotation rule
explain: Modern Windows blocks insecure guest authentication to shares and printers by default, so proper accounts are required.

q: After a second monitor is disconnected, windows open on a screen that is no longer attached. How can a user recover a lost window?
options: Select the app on the taskbar, then press Alt+Space and Move, or use Win+arrow keys, to bring it back
Reinstall the application so it forgets its previous window position and opens centered on the main display
Clear the display configuration cache by removing and re-adding the second monitor in Device Manager settings
Reset the display adapter's saved multi-monitor layout by disabling and re-enabling it in Device Manager
explain: Off-screen windows retain their old coordinates, and the system Move command or Win+arrow keys bring them onto a live display.

q: A laptop's compact keyboard types numbers when letter keys on the right side are pressed. What is the cause?
options: A virus has remapped the right side of the keyboard layout to send numeric scan codes to applications
A failing hard drive is corrupting the keyboard driver settings that control the embedded keypad layer
The wrong Windows language pack has been applied, changing the right-side letter keys to a numeric layout
Num Lock is on, activating the embedded numeric keypad layer; use Fn+NumLock to toggle it
explain: Many compact laptops overlay a numeric keypad on letter keys, and Num Lock state activates that layer.

q: A gamer keeps opening the Sticky Keys prompt mid-game when tapping Shift. What is the correct fix?
options: Replace the keyboard with a model that has no Shift key shortcut
Disable the Shift key entirely in the Windows keyboard settings
Turn off the 'press Shift five times' shortcut in Accessibility keyboard settings
Reinstall the game so it captures the Shift key before Windows
explain: The Sticky Keys activation shortcut can be disabled in Accessibility settings without disabling the feature itself.

q: Desktop icons have all disappeared, but the files are still in the Desktop folder. What is the likely cause?
options: The files were deleted from view by the latest Windows Update
'Show desktop icons' was toggled off, or a tablet or rotation state changed the view
The hard drive failed and is showing only the folder contents
OneDrive permanently deleted the icons during its last sync
explain: Icon visibility is a desktop view setting, and the underlying files usually remain untouched when it is toggled off.

q: The taskbar search box does nothing when typing. What is a quick service-level check for this problem?
options: Restart the Windows Search service and the CTF Loader (ctfmon) for text input
Format the system drive and rebuild the search index from scratch
Replace the keyboard because search input uses a special driver
Disable the firewall profile that is blocking taskbar search input
explain: Taskbar search depends on the Search service for results and ctfmon for text input, so restarting both often revives it.

q: A dual-boot Windows/Linux user finds Windows time is wrong by several hours after using Linux. What is the correct fix?
options: Replace the CMOS battery every month so the hardware clock holds the correct local time between boots
Disable NTP time synchronization in both operating systems so neither one adjusts the hardware clock
Set the Windows time zone to UTC for all dual-boot computers regardless of the user's local time zone
Tell Linux to use local time, or set Windows' RealTimeIsUniversal, because Linux defaults the hardware clock to UTC
explain: Linux keeps the hardware clock in UTC while Windows expects local time, so aligning one side ends the conflict.

q: Windows Spotlight is stuck on the same lock-screen image for weeks. What is a common reset for this problem?
options: Replace the monitor because its firmware is caching the previous lock-screen image between Windows sessions
Reinstall Windows to reset all lock-screen personalization settings, content packages, and image caches at once
Re-register or reset the Spotlight content settings by clearing its cache under the ContentDeliveryManager package
Disable the lock screen entirely so Spotlight no longer needs to download or rotate its background images
explain: A corrupt Spotlight cache freezes image rotation, and resetting the package data restarts fresh downloads.

q: The widgets panel uses notable CPU and memory on a work PC. What is the cleanest fix for this overhead?
options: Add more RAM before changing any Windows feature settings
Turn off Widgets from taskbar settings, or by policy on managed machines
Disable Windows Update so the widgets panel stops refreshing content
Delete the taskbar so the widgets panel cannot be launched
explain: Widgets run web content continuously, so disabling the feature removes the overhead.

q: A laptop offers no Sleep option in the power menu after a driver change. What usually restores it?
options: Restoring power plan defaults and ensuring graphics and chipset drivers support modern standby states
Deleting the page file so Windows rebuilds its power configuration and standby state tables at the next boot
Fully draining the battery several times to recalibrate which sleep states the firmware reports to Windows
Disabling Hibernate only, which forces the Sleep option back into the power menu for all local user accounts
explain: Missing sleep states are usually driver or power-plan issues, and powercfg /a shows which states the platform supports.

q: Hibernate is missing from the shutdown options. How can it be re-enabled?
options: Run chkdsk with a hibernate switch to rebuild the hibernation file
Set a BIOS password so the firmware exposes hibernation options
Defragment the system drive so hiberfil.sys can be created contiguously
Run powercfg /hibernate on, then check Hibernate in 'Choose what the power buttons do'
explain: Hibernation must be enabled with powercfg before its shutdown-menu checkbox becomes available.

q: Airplane mode appears stuck on and its toggle is greyed out. After a reboot, what should be checked next?
options: The printer driver, because it manages wireless device queues in Windows
The Recycle Bin, because stuck wireless settings are stored there temporarily
Device Manager, to re-enable the radio collection device, and the Radio Management Service
Disk quotas, because a full quota can disable wireless radio controls
explain: A disabled airplane-mode collection device or a stuck Radio Management Service leaves radios off with a greyed toggle.

q: Windows Hello face sign-in fails with 'camera not found' although the webcam works in apps. What is a likely conflict?
options: The monitor brightness is set too low for the IR camera to capture enough detail for face recognition sign-in
Another app or the antivirus is blocking the Hello IR camera, or the biometric service needs restarting
The user's glasses reflect the IR illuminator, which prevents Hello from matching the face at every sign-in try
The Wi-Fi channel in use is interfering with the camera's USB connection to the Windows Hello service process
explain: Hello uses the IR camera through a protected path, so security software blocks and biometric service faults are common causes.

q: After a feature update, several users report the Start menu will not open. What is a standard repair?
options: Re-register the Shell Experience and Start menu packages for the affected profiles via PowerShell
Replace every affected user's keyboard because the update changed how Start menu keystrokes are processed
Roll back the domain controllers because the update altered how shell packages register for domain accounts
Disable search indexing domain-wide to relieve the Start menu service while it rebuilds its package database
explain: Corrupted shell package registrations break Start, and re-registering the AppX shell components repairs it.

q: File Explorer keeps crashing and restarting when opening a folder with videos. What is a probable cause?
options: The folder contains too many files for Explorer to enumerate reliably
The monitor cable is loose and interrupts Explorer's video rendering
Windows activation has expired and disabled video folder previews
A faulty thumbnail handler or shell extension, or a corrupt thumbnail cache
explain: Shell extensions hook into Explorer, and disabling third-party handlers and clearing the thumbnail cache isolates the fault.

q: A specific website renders blank in Edge or Chrome but works in another browser. What are the best first steps?
options: Reinstall Windows to rebuild the browser's rendering engine, its profile store, and its network stack together
Call the website's ISP to report a browser-specific rendering fault affecting that site's hosted page content
Clear that site's cookies and cache and test in an InPrivate or Incognito window with extensions off
Disable the firewall permanently so the site can load all of its scripts, frames, and cached resources freely
explain: An InPrivate/Incognito test isolates extensions and cached data, the two most common single-browser causes.

q: Clicking links in emails opens the wrong browser even after defaults were set. What should be checked?
options: A stuck per-app default in the email client itself, which overrides the Windows default browser for its own links
The HTTP/HTTPS and .htm/.html associations specifically, because protocol handlers can differ from the default-browser summary
The mouse button mapping has been changed, so single clicks are registered as open-with commands for web links
The mail server's outbound processing is rewriting link targets before the messages reach the user's inbox folder
explain: Windows tracks per-protocol associations, and a stale HTTPS handler can keep stealing links from the chosen default browser.

q: An app opens with its window completely off-screen after undocking. Besides keyboard move tricks, what does Windows offer to recover it?
options: Cascade windows, or the display-settings 'make this my main display' reset, to force re-layout
Deleting the app's icon so Windows forgets its saved window position
Running Disk Cleanup to remove the cached display configuration files
Changing the time zone to force all application windows to redraw
explain: Undocking coordinate errors strand windows, and Cascade windows forces all windows onto visible displays.

q: Screen orientation flipped upside down after a cat walked on the keyboard. What is the quickest way to restore it?
options: Reinstalling the display driver to reset the orientation sensor calibration stored in its configuration data
Rotating the monitor physically and leaving it inverted because the panel's orientation cannot be set in software
Booting into Safe Mode only, because display orientation cannot be changed back during a normal Windows session
Press Ctrl+Alt+Up Arrow on supported Intel graphics, or set Orientation to Landscape in Display settings
explain: Graphics hotkeys rotate the display, and Display settings restore Landscape orientation on any system.

q: Touchpad gestures such as two-finger scroll stopped after an update. What is the correct fix path?
options: Replace the touchpad hardware before checking any software settings
Disable the external mouse so gestures are forced back to the touchpad
Reinstall the precision touchpad driver and check that touchpad gestures are enabled in Settings
Format the drive to remove the update that changed gesture behavior
explain: Gesture support lives in the touchpad driver and its Settings page, and updates can reset both.

q: A mouse pointer drifts on its own in small movements on a laptop. What is a frequent cause?
options: The monitor refresh rate is set too high for the pointer driver to track movement smoothly on the desktop
A failing or dirty touchpad registers phantom input; disable the touchpad while a mouse is connected to test
A strong Wi-Fi signal is interfering with the wireless mouse receiver's pointer positioning data packets
The screensaver is injecting small pointer movements while the system waits for its idle activation timer
explain: Phantom touchpad input is a classic cause of pointer drift, and isolating the touchpad confirms hardware versus software.

q: Windows reports 'No audio output device is installed' after an update, though the hardware is fine in BIOS. What is the correct fix?
options: Reinstall the audio driver and confirm the Windows Audio service is running, checking for a broken generic driver from the update
Replace the speakers because the update permanently damaged their firmware while installing the new driver
Reinstall Windows immediately before testing whether the vendor audio driver restores the missing device
Disable Secure Boot so the updated audio driver can load without signature verification at system startup
explain: Updates can install a broken generic audio driver, and restoring the vendor driver plus checking the Audio service restores sound.

q: One user cannot print to any printer, while others on the same PC can print normally. What should be tested first?
options: Whether all the printers on the network failed at the same time for every user account on every computer
Whether the network connection is down for the entire office, which would affect all users and all printers
Whether toner is empty in every printer the user could select, which would block all of their print jobs
Whether the fault follows the profile: sign in as another user to isolate profile settings or credentials from a machine fault
explain: Profile-scoped faults follow the user, while machine faults affect every account on the computer.

q: A mapped network drive shows a red X at logon but works when clicked. What does this usually indicate?
options: A failing hard drive is corrupting the mapped drive's stored connection data in the user's local profile
A virus is disconnecting the mapped drive at every logon and restoring it when the user clicks its icon
A timing artifact: Explorer maps the drive before the network is fully ready, and it reconnects on access
A broken network cable is intermittently interrupting the drive mapping handshake during the logon process
explain: A red X at logon is a long-standing cosmetic reconnect timing issue rather than data loss.

q: Windows time keeps drifting on a domain PC even after manual correction. What should be investigated?
options: The monitor's internal clock, which supplies time to the operating system
The time service (w32time) source and domain hierarchy, where the PDC emulator is the authority
The user's wristwatch, to confirm the drift is real and not perceived
The screensaver settings, which can pause the system clock display
explain: Domain members sync from the domain controller hierarchy, and a broken w32time configuration also breaks Kerberos and logging.

q: A PC wakes instantly every time it is put to sleep. Which command finds the culprit?
options: powercfg /lastwake, together with /waketimers and the device wake-armed lists
ipconfig /wake, to display the last network wake event source address
chkdsk /sleep, to scan the disk for sleep-related file errors overnight
msconfig /wake, to list startup items that can wake the computer remotely
explain: powercfg reports the last wake source, which is usually a network adapter, USB device, or scheduled timer.

q: Clipboard history (Win+V) does not work for one user. How is it enabled or fixed?
options: Reinstall Notepad, because clipboard history depends on its components
Change the mouse settings that control clipboard paste shortcuts in Windows
Run Disk Cleanup to clear the clipboard history database files from the disk
In Settings under System > Clipboard, turn on Clipboard history and check policy on managed devices
explain: Clipboard history is off by default in some builds and can be controlled by policy, so its Settings toggle is the fix.

q: The Snipping Tool shortcut (Win+Shift+S) stopped working. What are the common fixes?
options: Buy a new keyboard because the shortcut requires dedicated screenshot keys that standard keyboards lack
Reinstall Windows to restore the default screenshot shortcut registrations and the Snipping Tool package
Repair or Reset the Snipping Tool app in Settings and verify the Print Screen key setting in Accessibility
Disable OneDrive because it intercepts the screenshot shortcut to save captures to the user's cloud folder
explain: App corruption and the Print Screen-to-snip toggle are the frequent causes of a broken Win+Shift+S shortcut.

q: A user's Recycle Bin constantly reports corruption on one drive. What is the correct repair?
options: Format the drive so Windows can recreate all of its system folders
Delete the hidden $Recycle.Bin folder for that drive from an elevated prompt so Windows recreates it
Disable the Recycle Bin forever so the corruption prompts stop appearing
Reinstall Explorer from the Microsoft Store to rebuild the Recycle Bin
explain: A damaged per-drive recycle store produces repeated corruption prompts, and deleting it lets Windows recreate a clean one.

q: Thumbnails no longer preview photos in Explorer. What should be checked?
options: Folder Options and Performance settings: 'Always show icons, never thumbnails' is off, and clear the thumbnail cache
The graphics card temperature, because overheating disables thumbnail previews first
The user's wallpaper, because a corrupt wallpaper blocks folder thumbnail rendering
The default printer, because Explorer uses it to render image thumbnails on screen
explain: A single view checkbox or a corrupt thumbnail cache kills previews while the files themselves remain fine.

q: Opening any folder spawns a brand-new Explorer window. Which setting controls this behavior?
options: A ransomware infection that forces every folder into its own process window
The double-click speed setting for the mouse in Windows Settings
The screen resolution, which limits how many folders share one window
Folder Options 'Open each folder in the same window' on the General tab
explain: An Explorer browsing option causes the new-window behavior, and restoring 'same window' corrects it.

q: A Microsoft Store app crashes instantly on launch after an update. What is the built-in repair sequence?
options: Format the drive and reinstall the app from the Microsoft Store afterward
Delete the user's profile so the app registers under a fresh account state
Disable Windows Update so the app cannot receive another broken update
In Settings under Apps, open the app's Advanced options: try Repair first, then Reset if needed
explain: Repair keeps app data while Reset wipes local state, which is the escalation path for Store apps.

q: An MSI installation fails with error 1603. What is the technician's best next step?
options: Reboot the computer ten times to clear the generic installation error
Disable the firewall permanently so the installer can complete its actions
Run the install with verbose logging (/L*v) or check the MSI log in %temp% to find the failing action
Ignore the error because 1603 indicates a successful but silent installation
explain: Error 1603 is a generic fatal error, and the verbose MSI log names the custom action or prerequisite that actually failed.

q: A user sees 'This app can't run on your PC' for a freshly downloaded program. What are the most common causes?
options: The monitor is too old to display the program's user interface correctly
An architecture mismatch (32-bit vs 64-bit or ARM) or the PC being in S mode
The downloaded file is too small to contain a complete working program
The PC needs a new IP address before it can run downloaded programs
explain: The download must match the CPU architecture, and S mode blocks non-Store software from running.

q: An application works when run as administrator but fails for a standard user. What is usually the real problem?
options: The app writes to protected locations such as Program Files or HKLM; fix permissions or update the app instead of running as admin forever
The user needs a new PC because their standard account is permanently unable to run this legacy application
The app is a virus using admin rights to write its payload into protected system folders at every launch
The keyboard layout is preventing the app from reading its configuration file from its protected folder
explain: Legacy apps that assume admin rights break under standard accounts, and shims or vendor updates are the durable fix.

q: Outlook reports it cannot open the OST and suggests deleting it. Why is deleting an OST safe?
options: Because OSTs contain the only copy of the user's email and deleting them archives it
Because deleting the OST forces a Windows reinstall that repairs Outlook profiles
Because deleting the OST deletes the mailbox, which removes the corruption at the server
Because it is a local cached copy that Outlook rebuilds from the Exchange or Microsoft 365 server
explain: An OST is an offline cache, unlike a PST archive, so a corrupt OST can be deleted and resynchronized from the server.

q: Outlook search suddenly returns no results for recent mail. What is the correct fix path?
options: Delete the OST every time search results appear incomplete for recent messages
Disable Windows Search permanently so Outlook uses its own slower search method
Check Outlook's indexing status and rebuild the search index under Indexing Options
Reinstall Windows to rebuild the search catalog and Outlook profile together
explain: Outlook search rides the Windows Search index, so a stuck or corrupt index is rebuilt rather than the mailbox.

q: Outlook is stuck showing 'Disconnected' though the network is fine. What is a commonly overlooked cause?
options: The monitor fell asleep and paused Outlook's connection status updates
Work Offline mode was toggled on, which is found on the Send/Receive tab
The OST file is too new for Outlook to trust its synchronized contents
The user has too many folders, which always disconnects the mailbox session
explain: Work Offline survives restarts and mimics a server outage while the network is actually fine.

q: Word and Excel start very slowly and sometimes hang. What is a leading suspect and how is it tested?
options: A faulty third-party COM add-in; test by starting the app in its Safe Mode, such as winword /safe
The printer driver color profile, which delays every Office application launch
The Windows theme, which renders slowly in Office's title bar and ribbon
The mouse polling rate, which overwhelms Office during its startup sequence
explain: Office Safe Mode disables add-ins, so re-enabling them one at a time identifies the offending add-in.

q: PowerPoint presentations show substituted fonts on a colleague's PC. How should the author prevent this?
options: Save the presentation as PDF only so fonts can never be substituted again
Increase the file size manually so the fonts have room to be included
Compress the file into a ZIP archive so the fonts travel with the slides
Embed fonts in the file under Save options, or use standard fonts available on both PCs
explain: Font embedding, where licenses allow, travels the typefaces with the presentation to other computers.

q: A corrupt Normal.dotm template causes Word to crash on launch. What is the correct fix?
options: Reinstall Windows to replace the global Word template and its registry keys
Delete all documents in the user's Documents folder that use the template
Rename or delete Normal.dotm; Word recreates a clean one at its next start
Disable macros forever so the template is never loaded by Word again
explain: A damaged global template breaks every Word launch, and renaming it lets Word regenerate a clean copy.

q: A browser's default search engine changed itself and results are full of ads. After removing the culprit extension, what else must be done?
options: Buy a premium browser whose search engine settings cannot be changed by extensions or injected web content
Reset the browser's search engine and shortcut settings, scan for malware, and check browser shortcut targets for appended URLs
Reset the DNS settings because the hijacker changed the resolver that returns the ad-filled search results
Disable DNS on the adapter so the hijacked search engine can no longer resolve its ad-serving result pages
explain: Hijackers persist through extensions, settings, and modified shortcuts, so all three must be checked and a malware scan run.

q: Every HTTPS site shows 'Your connection is not private' on one PC only, starting today. What should be checked first?
options: The system date and time, because a wrong clock invalidates certificates
The ISP's website, to confirm whether it has revoked site certificates
The Wi-Fi password, because an expired password breaks certificate validation
The browser theme, because a corrupt theme can block secure page rendering
explain: Certificate validity periods depend on the system clock, so a reset clock breaks every secure site at once.

q: After malware cleanup, browsers cannot load any pages but ping works. Which leftover setting should be checked?
options: The hosts file wallpaper entry that malware added during the infection cleanup
The Recycle Bin contents that malware left behind on the system drive
The page file size, which malware changed to block browser page loading
A bogus proxy configured in Internet Settings, and reset the WinHTTP proxy with netsh winhttp reset proxy
explain: Malware often points browsers at a dead proxy, and that setting survives the malware's removal until it is cleared.

q: Chrome reports every download as 'Virus scan failed' after an antivirus change. What is usually the cause?
options: All downloaded files really are infected, because the new antivirus detects threats the old one missed in scans
The hard drive is full, so Chrome cannot write downloaded files or complete their post-download virus scans
The registered antivirus attachment-scan integration is broken; repair or reinstall the AV or adjust Chrome's scan settings
